nodes.heading: PART 1—PRELIMINARY
nodes.text: PART 1—PRELIMINARY
Part 1 sets out the purpose of the Bill, how the purpose will be achieved and when the Bill will commence.
outlines the purpose of the Bill.
states how the purpose will be achieved.

provides that, with the exception of a provision relating to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987, the Bill or provisions of the Bill will commence on 1 October 2009 if it is, or they are, not proclaimed before that date.

nodes.heading: PART 2—INTERPRETATION
nodes.text: PART 2—INTERPRETATION

Part 2 defines the key words and phrases used in the Bill.  In particular, this Part sets out who is considered a "family member" and what behaviour is considered "family violence" in order to obtain the protection of an order.
defines certain words and phrases used in the Bill.  Of particular note is that safety is defined broadly to mean "safety from family violence".

defines the meaning of family violence.  This definition is significant as under clause 74 an affected family member must have experienced family violence to obtain the protection of an order.  This definition has been included in response to a VLRC recommendation that a legislative definition of family violence would assist with interpreting and applying the Bill.

provides a general definition of behaviour that is family violence.  This includes behaviour that causes a child to hear, witness or otherwise be exposed to family violence. To assist with interpretation this subclause provides some non-exclusive examples of behaviour that may expose a child to family violence.  These examples clarify that a respondent does not need to intend a child to hear, witness or otherwise be exposed to family violence.  It is sufficient if any of these things result from the respondent's actions.

provides some non-exclusive examples of behaviour that is family violence.  This clause is intended to guide those using the Bill as to what sorts of behaviour are covered by the general definition in clause 5(1).  There are other forms of behaviour that will come within the scope of clause 5(1) that are not listed in this subclause.

provides that behaviour may be considered family violence for the purpose of this Bill even if it is not a criminal offence.  An example of a non-criminal form of family violence may be emotionally or psychologically abusive behaviour.

provides a definition of economic abuse, a term that is used in the definition of family violence.  To guide interpretation of the general definition of economic abuse, this clause includes some non-exhaustive examples of behaviour that may constitute economic abuse.  The majority of these examples have been drawn from the Tasmanian Family Violence Act 2004.

provides a definition of emotional or psychological abuse, a term that is used in the definition of family violence.  To guide interpretation of the general definition of emotional or psychological abuse, this clause includes some non-exhaustive examples of behaviour that may constitute emotional or psychological abuse.  These examples have been drawn, in part, from findings of research into family violence that shows that these forms of emotional or psychological abuse are particularly common in violent relationships.
defines the term family member.  This definition is significant as under clause 74 an affected person must have experienced violence from a family member to obtain the protection of an order.
provides a list of relationships that are automatically considered family.

clarifies that a relationship does not need to be sexual in order to be an intimate personal relationship. An example of an intimate personal relationship of this type may be a dating relationship between adolescents.

provides that relationships not covered by clause 8(1) may also be a family relationship for the purposes of this Bill if the person regarded the person as being like a family member and the court believes it is reasonable to consider the person as being like a family member.  The subclause provides a list of factors for the court to consider when determining whether it is reasonable to regard the person as being like a family member.  These factors are partly drawn from section 35(2) of the Relationships Act 2008.  Additional factors have also been included, as this clause relates to a family like relationship, rather than the narrower concept of domestic partnership under the Relationships Act 2008.
clarifies that the relationship must be considered in its entirety when the court is deciding whether a person is a family member.

defines the meaning of domestic partner for the purpose of clause 8.  This definition of domestic partner is drawn from the Relationships Act 2008 which made consequential amendments to all Victorian Acts that refer to domestic partners to provide a consistent definition.
outlines which relationships are considered a relative for the purpose of the Bill.
clarifies that where a person is a domestic partner, a relative includes any person who would have been a relative if the domestic partners were married.
provides a definition of a family violence intervention order, final order and interim order.

nodes.heading: PART 3—POLICE PROTECTION BEFORE COURT
nodes.text: PART 3—POLICE PROTECTION BEFORE COURT

Part 3 provides police officers with protective powers prior to an intervention order being made.  It includes a power for police to hold a person while protective measures are being put in place and issue a family violence safety notice prior to the court considering an application for a family violence intervention order.

provides for definitions for the purposes of this Division.
The definition of directed person means a person who is or has been subject to a direction under clause 14.
provides the criteria for the exercise of powers under clause 14. These criteria are—
that the police officer intends to apply for either a family violence intervention order (or a variation of such an order) or a family violence safety notice; and
the officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the person is at least 18 years old; and

the officer believes on reasonable grounds that the exercise of these powers is necessary to ensure the safety of the affected family member or to preserve their property.  This is similar to the grounds for the court making an interim intervention order under clause 53(1)(a) or issuing a warrant for arrest with an application for a family violence intervention order under clause 50.
provides how a police officer may exercise the direction power if criteria in clause 13 are satisfied.  It provides a police officer may direct a person to—
remain at the place where the person is when the direction is given; or
go to, and remain at, a place stated by the officer; or
remain in the company of—
the police officer; or
another police officer stated in the direction; or
another person stated by the police officer.
The direction may be given orally or in writing.
provides that a direction to remain in the company of another person who is not a police officer may only be given with that person's consent.
provides that a direction under clause 14(1) must be reasonable in the circumstances.

provides that, at the time of giving the direction, the police officer must inform the directed person that refusing or failing to comply with the direction may result in their apprehension and detention under clause 15 and that, if apprehended and detained under that clause, it is an offence to escape or attempt to escape.  This offence is provided in section 49E of the Summary Offences Act 1966 and a note at the foot of clause 15(2) refers to this offence.
provides a detention power where a person refuses or fails to comply with a direction under clause 14.

provides that a police officer may use such force as is reasonably necessary to apprehend and detain a person directed under clause 14 where that person refuses or fails to comply with that direction.

provides that a person may be detained at a police station or other place.  A person may only be detained at a police gaol (within the meaning of the Corrections Act 1986) where the police officer considers this location is necessary for the protection of any person or property or to prevent the person escaping from detention.
ensures that the offence in section 479C of the Crimes Act 1958 does not apply to a person who escapes or attempts to escape from detention.

provides police officers with a power to search a person if the person has been apprehended and detained under the holding powers provided in Division 1 of Part 3.  A police officer may conduct a search if the officer suspects the person may possess something that could cause injury or damage or be used to escape.  This is to ensure that if a person is to be detained police officers have the power to remove any items that could be used by the person to harm themselves or another person.

provides that a police officer cannot search a person under this clause if the officer only suspects that the search would provide evidence of an offence.  This is because the detention power is to be used to protect persons experiencing family violence and is not a criminal detention power. Police officers do have a power to search for evidence of a crime  if under the Crimes Act 1958 or common law search powers are met.
provides some procedural requirements for persons who are under a clause 14 direction at a police station and persons under a clause 15 detention.

provides an obligation on police officers to inform the detained person of certain persons they may communicate or attempt to communicate with, and provides for a prescribed form to be given to the detained person containing prescribed information about their rights and responsibilities under Division 1 of Part 3.
The persons with whom they may communicate or attempt to communicate are—
a friend or relative (other than the affected  family member) to inform them of their whereabouts; and
a legal practitioner.
provides that if a detained person does wish to communicate with any of these people, a police officer must—
afford the person reasonable facilities as soon as practicable to enable the communication; and
allow the person's legal practitioner or a clerk of the legal practitioner to communicate with the person in circumstances where, as far as practicable, the communication will not be overheard.
clarifies that clause 17(4) does not allow the detained person to communicate with the affected family member, consistent with clause 17(2)(a)(i).

seeks to ensure that access to a competent interpreter is arranged for people who do not have knowledge of the English language that is sufficient to enable them to understand the reason for the direction or detention.

provides that a police officer does not have to comply with clauses 17(2) and (4) where the officer reasonably believes that such communication may jeopardise the safety of the affected family member or their property.
provides limits on how long the direction or detention may continue.

limits the duration of the direction power, inclusive of the detention power if it has been invoked, to 6 hours from the time the initial direction is given, or for a further period if ordered by the court under clause 19.  A further period ordered by the court under new clause 19 may not allow the total period of direction, inclusive of any detention period, to continue beyond 10 hours.
provides that, despite clause 18(1), the direction or detention ceases upon any one of a number of circumstances. These circumstances are—
a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order being served on the directed person; or
the directed person being arrested under a warrant issued under clause 50; or
the police officer determining not to make, or to withdraw, an application for a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order.

provides that, despite clause 18(2), where a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order is served on the directed person, the direction or detention may continue if the directing officer believes on reasonable grounds that its continuation is necessary to enable further measures to be taken for the protection of the affected family member. The further measures are limited to those that are for the protection of the affected family member, but the police officer giving the direction must also believe the continuation of the direction or detention is necessary to ensure the safety of the affected family member or to preserve the property of the affected family member.

provides that the direction or detention also ceases if a family violence safety notice application, family violence intervention order application or application for warrant under clause 50 of the Bill is refused.

, however, provides that if a warrant under clause 50 is refused or a family violence safety notice application is refused but an application for the intervention order has not yet been determined by the court on an interim basis, or withdrawn by the police officer, or an application for a family violence intervention order is intended to be made in place of the family violence safety notice application, the direction power continues until it ceases because any of the other grounds in clauses 18(1), (2), (3) or (4)(a) are satisfied.

allows a police officer to apply to the court for an extension of the period of the direction or detention beyond 6 hours. However, such extension applications cannot be made where the police officer is applying for a family violence safety notice. The application must be made within 6 hours after the direction is given and the court may only grant an extension of time where satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances.  The extension of time must not be for a period that would cause the total period of direction, inclusive of any detention period, to continue beyond 10 hours.

provides for the application to the court for an extension of the period of the direction, or detention, to be made by telephone, facsimile machine or other electronic communication.  The procedure for this application largely mirrors that provided for urgent family violence intervention order applications sought by telephone, facsimile and electronic communications in clause 44 where applicable; however, an application under clause 20 may be made if the police officer reasonably believes that it is impracticable to make the application in person.
requires a police officer to notify the person under the direction or detention when such power ceases and immediately release the person if they are detained.
also provides that the police officer must take reasonable steps to notify the protected person or affected family member that the direction has ended.
prohibits a police officer from interviewing or questioning a person under the direction or detention in relation to any offence or alleged offence.
provides that the court may, if practicable, hear a person who is under the direction or detention, or an affected family member, or both, on the hearing of—
an application for a family violence intervention order; and
an application for an extension order under clause 19 (regardless of whether that application is made in person or by telephone or facsimile under clause 20).
Division 2—Family violence safety notices

outlines the circumstances in which a police officer may apply to another police officer of the rank of Sergeant or above for a family violence safety notice.
Clauses 24(a) to (d) provide that a police officer may only apply for a family violence safety notice if the police officer has reasonable grounds to suspect that the respondent is an adult without a cognitive impairment and that there is no family violence intervention order already on foot between the relevant parties.  The police officer also must have no reasonable grounds for suspecting that there is Family Law Act order or child protection order as defined by section 515(1) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 in place.  It is intended that if the respondent is a child, has a cognitive impairment or there are any of the listed orders on foot, the police officer will contact the Magistrates' Court to apply for an interim order under clause 44 or seek an urgent interim variation to the existing family violence intervention order (see clause 101).

provides the grounds for a family violence safety notice to be issued.  These grounds are the same as those required for an interim order under clause 53(1)(a).  These grounds constitute the circumstances that necessitate the provision of protection.  Thus, such notices are intended to provide protection where it is needed immediately until an application for a final order can be determined by the court.

states that the application may only be made after normal court hours.  If a police officer attends an incident during court hours it is intended that the police officer will make an application for an interim order at the court in accordance with clause 53 or, in appropriate circumstances, seek a warrant to arrest (see clause 50).  The family violence safety notice system has been created to provide immediate protection if the court is closed and the normal court processes cannot be accessed.
provides that an application for a family violence safety notice can be made in person or by fax, telephone or electronic communication.
covers how the police officer who receives the application makes a decision about whether to issue the family violence safety notice.

outlines the grounds that the officer must be satisfied of before issuing a family violence safety notice. These grounds are the same as those for the officer in determining whether to apply for the notice under clauses 24(d) and (e).

provides that the police officer making the decision must hear the police officer who has responded to the incident and may hear the respondent or the affected family member. This is to ensure procedural fairness while recognising that hearing all parties will not always be practical due to the urgent nature of the application.

provides what needs to be included in documentation if a police officer applies for the family violence safety notice in person and what needs to be documented if a police officer applies for a family violence safety notice by fax, telephone or electronic communication (defined as a safety notice form).

(a) provides that if a police officer is applying by fax, telephone or electronic communication for the family violence safety notice, the police officer issuing the family violence safety notice must complete an authorisation form including certain key information.

provides that as soon as practicable after the issue of a family violence safety notice applied for by fax, telephone or electronic communication, a police officer of the rank of Sergeant or higher must check the authorisation form against the safety notice form and if they are consistent, certify the safety notice form as accurate.

(b) provides that if there is a material discrepancy between the authorisation form and the safety notice form this should be rectified.  Clause 34 provides for service of the rectified safety notice form on the respondent.
(c) provides that the safety notice form (as corrected if necessary) must be then be certified as consistent with the authorisation form.

provides what would constitute a material discrepancy which would require correction under clause 28(2)(b).  The intention is to demonstrate that, for example, a typographical error or spelling mistake in the name of a respondent would not be sufficient to invalidate a condition of a safety notice form as provided for in clause 28(4).

provides that if there is a material discrepancy between the safety notice form and the authorisation form, the safety notice form is invalid but only to the extent of the inconsistency with the authorisation form.
provides the conditions that may be included in a family violence safety notice.

states that the conditions that may be included are the same as those that may be included on a family violence intervention order under clause 81, except for conditions that cancel or suspend a firearms authority or weapons approval. If the respondent has a firearms authority or weapons approval, it is intended that the responding police officer will use their powers under clause 163 to seize any firearms or weapons. The court will then consider whether to impose conditions under clause 81(2)(g) or (h) when the application for a family violence intervention order is considered.

provides for the duration of a family violence safety notice and makes clear that it starts when it is originally served on the respondent, even if it is subsequently corrected and re-served on the respondent.  The family violence safety notice ends either when the court refuses to make either an interim or final intervention order on the first mention date or, if the court makes a family violence intervention order on the first mention date, when that order is served on the respondent.

provides that the family violence safety notice is taken to be an application for a family violence intervention order by the police officer who applied for the family violence safety notice and a summons for the respondent to appear at the first mention date.

sets out that the first mention date must be within 72 hours of the service of the family violence safety notice unless a public holiday makes this impossible. In such cases, the first mention will take place on the next working day after the public holiday.

outlines the information that must be included in a family violence safety notice.  These matters are included to ensure that the respondent and person protected by the notice understand the nature and consequences of the notice.

provides that the police officer must ask the respondent for an address to be used for service.  The respondent is not obliged to comply with this request.  This requirement has been included to assist police to serve any future documents, such as a family violence intervention order, particularly if police are removing the respondent from the residence.

provides that as soon as practicable after the family violence safety notice is issued, a police officer must serve a copy of the family violence safety notice on the respondent and protected person.  If the family violence safety notice is a safety notice form and it has been corrected, then this corrected document must be served.

(i) then provides that if the family violence safety notice was issued on an application made in person, then a copy of the form completed under clause 27(1) by the police officer issuing the family violence safety notice must be filed with the Magistrates' Court.

(ii) provides that if a family violence safety notice was issued on an application by fax, telephone or electronic communication under clause 25(b) then a copy of the safety notice form certified as accurate under clause 28(2)(c) must be filed with the Magistrates' Court.
outlines how a police officer must explain a family violence safety notice.

provides that the police officer who serves the family violence safety notice must also provide an explanation of the notice and take reasonable steps to ensure the person understands the nature and consequences of the notice. For example, a police officer would be expected to explain and answer questions a respondent or protected person has about the effect of the notice.
outlines matters that must be included in the explanation to ensure that the respondent and protected person are informed of the most relevant matters.
provides that the police officer must use an interpreter to provide an explanation under this clause if the person does not have a sufficient understanding of English.
provides that if an explanation is not given in accordance with this clause the notice is still valid.
outlines a police officer's obligations in relation to the accommodation of the respondent or protected person.

states that where a notice excludes the respondent from the residence, the police officer must then consider the accommodation needs of the respondent and any dependent children and take any reasonable steps to ensure those affected have access to temporary accommodation.  An example of a reasonable step would be taking the respondent to a nearby friend's or relative's residence.  This requirement has been included to reduce the likelihood of the respondent returning to the residence in contravention of the safety notice.

states that if a notice does not include an exclusion condition, the police officer must consider the accommodation needs of the protected person and any dependent children and take any reasonable steps to ensure those affected have access to temporary accommodation.  An example of a reasonable step would be taking the protected person to a nearby friend's or relative's residence.  This subclause has been included to ensure that if a protected person wishes to leave the residence or a formal police risk assessment indicates it is unsafe for the protected person to stay, the attending police officer has an obligation to take any reasonable steps to allow the protected person to do so.

provides that there is no obligation on police officers to provide free accommodation for those affected by a family violence safety notice.  This subclause has been included as temporary accommodation services vary in their availability across Victoria and there may not be any appropriate temporary accommodation that the police officer can access.

provides that it is an offence to contravene a family violence safety notice.  The maximum penalty for this offence is a maximum of 240 penalty units and or 2 years imprisonment. This penalty level was informed by a report of the Sentencing Advisory Council, Report on Maximum Penalties for Breaches of Intervention Orders.

provides that a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant if the officer believes on reasonable grounds that the person has contravened a family violence safety notice. This power of arrest without a warrant has been provided to provide further protection to the person protected by the notice. It is the same arrest power as that provided by clause 124 where a police officer believes a person has contravened a family violence intervention order.  The Bail Act 1977 will apply to those arrested under this power.

provides that if, despite the criteria set out in clause 24, a police officer issues a family violence safety notice when there is a family violence intervention order on foot, then the family violence intervention order prevails.

requires Victoria Police and the Magistrates' Court to provide reports to the Attorney-General about the operation of family violence safety notices 12 months after the commencement of this Division.  This is to ensure that statistical information is collected and made available to monitor and evaluate the operation of the new system.

provides that this Division expires two years after commencement.  The intention is that the effectiveness of the family violence safety notice system will be evaluated within this time to determine whether it is providing an effective form of protection outside court hours.

nodes.heading: PART 4—FAMILY VIOLENCE INTERVENTION ORDERS
nodes.text: PART 4—FAMILY VIOLENCE INTERVENTION ORDERS

Part 4 of the Bill sets out how an application for a family violence intervention order is made, how proceedings are conducted, the power of the court to make interim and final orders, the conditions that may be included in an order and how long an order will last.  Once an order has been made, this Part provides how it can be varied, revoked or extended.  This Part also outlines how a decision can be appealed and creates a criminal offence of contravening the conditions of a family violence intervention order.
Division 1—Application for family violence intervention order Division 1 sets out the processes and procedures involved in applying for an order.  In particular, this Division outlines who may apply for an order and how an application is made.

states that an application must be made at the proper venue of the Magistrates' Court or Children's Court.  Proper venue is defined in clause 4 by reference to the meaning in section 3(1) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 for the Magistrates' Court and section 3(1) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 for the Children's Court.

outlines how an application is to be made.  An application must include information that is prescribed under the rules made under this Bill.  It also must be sworn or affirmed or, in the case of a police officer, may be certified.
If the information in the application is sworn or affirmed, it will satisfy the requirements for evidence on an interim hearing under clause 55.

provides that an application may be made by telephone, fax or other electronic means outside of normal court hours or in remote areas if the application is made by a police officer. This clause may be used by police where the requirements outlined in clause 24 for applying for a family violence safety notice are not met.  Such situations may include where the respondent is a child or has a cognitive impairment or where the application is made within court hours in a remote area.

outlines who may apply for a family violence intervention order. A police officer is able to apply on behalf of an affected family member, however the final order available is limited by clause 75 (where the affected family member does not consent to the application).  An affected family member can apply in person or any other person can apply on their behalf with the affected family member's consent.  This is to ensure that affected family members can obtain an order without the need to involve the police or to have legal representation.  If the affected family member is a child, an application can be made by a parent, by another person with the written consent of the parent, or by the child if the child is of or above 14 years and the court has given leave.  This is to ensure that children are not usually applicants for orders and there is another person taking responsibility for bringing the application.  If the affected family member has a guardian, an application can be made by the guardian or by any other person with the leave of the court.  This is to ensure that guardians have the power to take protective action.
provides further guidance to the court when leave is sought to bring an application under clause 45.

provides that the court must grant leave if it is in the best interests of the affected family member to do so, if the affected family member is a person with a guardian or a child where the parent has given written consent.

provides that the court may only grant leave for a child of or above the age of 14 years if it is satisfied the child understands the nature and consequences of a family violence intervention order.  This is to ensure that applications for children are usually brought by another person, except in circumstances where the child has sufficient maturity to bring the matter themselves.
relates to applications for a child and the child's parent.

states that an application may be heard together for a child and the child's parent where the application arises from the same or similar circumstances.  This is to provide that families do not need to go through two separate hearings about similar matters, thereby reducing trauma from court proceedings and making the court process more efficient.
states that the matters may be heard separately if the applicant or respondent requests and the court thinks fit. The court must take into account any advantages of the matters being heard together.
outlines who must be served with the application for an order. This is to ensure that all relevant persons are aware of the application and can attend court on the first mention date.

provides that a registrar may issue a summons requiring the respondent to attend court once an application has been made. Failure to attend in answer to the summons is not an offence or breach of any bail conditions, but may result in a family violence intervention order being made in the absence of the respondent.

provides that a Magistrate or registrar may issue a warrant to arrest the respondent once an application for a family violence intervention order has been made.  Allowing a warrant to issue in these circumstances is another way for police to respond to family violence, particularly after hours, as bail conditions which protect the affected family member may be set.
provides the grounds for when a warrant may be issued.  A warrant may only be issued for an adult.
provides that a police officer can arrest a respondent even if the execution copy of the warrant is not in the police officer's possession.

states that when deciding whether to issue a warrant, the Magistrate or registrar must not take into account whether the person has been subject to a holding power under Division 1 of Part 3.  This is because the holding power is a civil power and its use should not prejudice the court's view of the respondent and the seriousness of the incident.  In addition, if a person is directed or detained and therefore under control whilst the warrant application is being determined, it may be difficult to satisfy the matters set out in clauses 50(1)(a) to (c) because the respondent does not constitute a threat while subject to holding powers.
provides the procedures for requesting a warrant.
outlines how the Bail Act 1977 applies if a warrant has been issued under clause 50.

provides that the Bail Act 1977 applies if a warrant has been issued as if the respondent were an accused person charged with an offence.  This means that once a warrant has been issued, a police officer or court must consider whether to grant bail or apply to have the respondent remanded in custody in accordance with the Bail Act 1977.  If bail is granted, conditions may be imposed.  For example, bail may include a condition to not approach or contact the affected family member.

provides that the affected family member must be advised of the outcome of the application for bail and, if bail is granted with any special conditions to protect the affected family member, the terms of those conditions.  The affected family member must also be given a copy of the undertaking of bail. This is to ensure the affected family member is aware of any conditions that restrict the respondent's behaviour and can report any violations of these conditions to the police.
Division 2—Interim orders
Division 2 outlines the circumstances in which an interim order may be made prior to the determination of an application for a final order and when an interim order expires.
provides the power for the court to make an interim order.
states that the court can make an interim order if there is an application for a family violence intervention order and—
the court is satisfied that an interim order is necessary; or
the parties consent to or do not oppose the making of an interim order; or
a family violence safety notice has been issued and the court is satisfied there are no circumstances that would justify discontinuing protection.

Subclause (2) provides that when making a decision about whether to make an interim order the court must not take into account whether the person has been subject to a holding power under Division 1 of Part 3.  This is because the holding power is a civil power and its use should not prejudice the court's view of the respondent and the seriousness of the incident.  In addition, if a person is directed or detained and therefore under control whilst the interim order is being considered, it may be difficult to satisfy the matters set out in clauses 53(1)(a) to (c) because the respondent does not constitute a threat while subject to holding powers.

provides that an interim order may be made if the respondent has not been served with the application or is not present in court. This is because an interim order is a temporary measure of protection prior to a final hearing for a family violence intervention order.

states that an application for an interim order must be supported by oral or affidavit evidence unless the application is made by electronic communication by a police officer and the requirement is waived.

provides that the court must not make an interim order without oral evidence or an affidavit unless the order is made by consent, the parties do not oppose the interim order being made or the application is made by electronic communication by a police officer.  This is to ensure that the court has been provided with evidence prior to making an interim order.  This is particularly important as an interim order can be made without the respondent being aware of the application (see clause 54).

provides that there is no obligation on the affected family member to give evidence in order to obtain an interim order.  Oral or affidavit evidence may be presented by, for example, a police officer who attended a family violence incident, a witness to an incident such as a friend or other family member, a medical professional who has treated the affected family member or any other person with relevant information to provide the court.  This is to ensure that if an affected family member does not feel able to provide evidence, the court can still consider any other relevant evidence and make an interim order for the affected family member's protection. If an application for a family violence intervention order is sworn or affirmed under clause 43, the requirement for affidavit evidence will be satisfied.

provides that an interim order can be made for the protection of more than one family member.  This is to ensure that the immediate protection of an interim order can apply to all affected family members and that separate court hearings do not need to be conducted for each family member.  For example, children of an affected family member could also be protected by an interim order under this clause.
outlines the court's obligations to explain the nature and consequences of an interim order.
provides that written explanation of the interim order must be given to the respondent and the affected family member and that this explanation must cover the listed matters.

outlines how the written explanation under clause 57(1) must be given to the respondent and protected person. This is to ensure that the explanation is received whether or not the persons attend court.
provides that a failure to provide the explanation does not make the interim order invalid.

outlines matters that the court must inform the police officer of if an interim order is made via telephone, fax or other electronic communication under clause 53.  This is to ensure that all relevant details are recorded by the police officer on the interim order.  A note draws attention to section 5(2) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 which provides that a court, constituted by a magistrate, may sit and act at any time and place in an attempt to clarify that a magistrate can make interim orders after hours even from their home.

provides that if an interim order is made, the matter should be listed for final determination as soon as practicable. This recognises that the interim order may have been made without the court hearing from the respondent.

outlines when an interim order will expire.  This clause ensures that the protection of an interim order will last until the court has determined whether to make a final order.  If the court makes a final order, the court may order that the interim protection continues until the final order has been served on the respondent. This is to ensure that there is no gap in protection for the affected family member while police locate the respondent to serve the final order.  The interim order expires if the court refuses to make a final order, revokes the interim order or if an application for the family violence intervention order is withdrawn prior to the final determination of the application.
Division 3—Proceedings for family violence intervention orders Division 3 outlines how the court will consider an application for a family violence intervention order, including how evidence may be presented.

provides the particular circumstances when a court can hear a contested application on a mention date.  It is expected that contested applications will not usually be heard on a mention date.  Rather they would be adjourned and listed as contested hearings to enable the parties to prepare their cases and arrange legal representation.  There may be some instances, however, when all parties wish a contested hearing to be heard and determined on the mention date.  To ensure no party feels pressured to have a contested hearing on a mention date, even if there is time to hear the matter, this clause sets out a list of matters the court must be satisfied about.  In particular—
that the parties have had the opportunity to seek legal advice;
all the parties to the proceeding consent to the contested hearing for the final determination taking place on the mention date; and
it is fair and just to all the parties to conduct the contested hearing on the mention date.
(a) provides that clause 61(1) does not stop the court making a final order on the mention date if all the parties consent to, or do not oppose, the making of the order.
(b) makes clear the court may make a final order on the mention date if the respondent has been served with the application but has not attended court on the mention date.

provides that a child who is not the applicant or respondent will not usually be legally represented.  The court must decide on its own initiative whether to allow the child to be represented and the parties cannot apply for the child to be separately represented.  The intention of this clause includes protecting children from being drawn into proceedings between their parents and forced to give their views separately to the parent who is seeking protection.  However, in some cases the child's interests may need to be separately represented from those of the child's parents and therefore the court may grant leave for separate representation.
provides that any number of applications may be heard together if the court thinks fit.  This is to ensure efficiency in the court process.

outlines how a person with a guardian may object to an application brought by the guardian on their behalf.  This clause is included to ensure that while a guardian has power under the Bill to apply for protection, the affected family member can also convey their views to the court.
concerns the rules of evidence for proceedings under the Bill.

states that, except as provided in the Bill, the court may inform itself in any way it thinks fit, despite any rules of evidence to the contrary, except in criminal matters where an order has been contravened.  This is particularly relevant for applicants and respondents who are not legally represented and means that the court may, for example, consider hearsay evidence.
provides that some provisions of the Evidence Act 1958 which provide protection for witnesses will continue to apply.

provides that the court may refuse to admit or limit the use of evidence if the court considers it is just and equitable to do so or if the probative value of the evidence may be outweighed by the danger that the evidence could be misleading, confusing or unfairly prejudicial.  This is to ensure that the removal of the rules of evidence does not unfairly prejudice a party to proceedings.

provides that evidence may be admitted via affidavit or sworn statement.  This is to ensure that witnesses do not need to attend the hearing to give their evidence in person.  However, a person can be required to attend court and be cross-examined on that evidence according to subclause (3).

provides that a child, other than an applicant or respondent for an order, must not give evidence in a proceeding unless given leave by the court.  In deciding whether to grant leave, the court must consider the need to protect children from unnecessary exposure to the court system and any harm that could occur to family relationships if a child was required to give evidence in the proceedings.

provides that the Magistrates' Court will have a discretion similar to that in section 126 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 to close court proceedings, or limit those who may attend, to protect a witness, affected family member or protected person from undue distress or embarrassment.  A penalty of 1000 penalty units or imprisonment for 3 months for contravention of an order under this section is provided to ensure parity with penalties under section 126 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 for similar offences.

provides alternative arrangements for conducting proceedings under the Bill.  These alternatives include the use of closed circuit television, permitting support persons while a person gives evidence and requiring legal representatives to remain seated.  A court may order the use of an alternative arrangement if a witness is an adult and must order the use of an alternative if the witness is a child unless it considers it inappropriate for a number of listed reasons.  In addition to this protection, clause 150 limits the circumstances in which a child can be present during a proceeding.
These alternative arrangements were originally enacted for use in the Family Violence Court Division only and were intended to make the experience of giving evidence in court easier for persons who had experienced family violence.  Similar provisions have also been enacted for witnesses in sexual offence matters in the Evidence Act 1958.  The VLRC found widespread support for making these arrangements available in all courts hearing family violence matters, not only specialist family violence courts.  This Bill also amends the Evidence Act 1958 to make these alternative ways of conducting hearings available in criminal prosecutions of family violence.
restricts personal cross-examination by the respondent of protected witnesses.

defines who is automatically considered a protected witness.  This includes those who are most likely to have experienced violence from the respondent—the affected family member and any other family members.  It also includes any child, as children are particularly vulnerable in the court process.

provides that any other person not listed in clause 70(1) may be declared a protected witness if the person has a cognitive impairment or otherwise needs the protection of the court.  This is to ensure that the court can provide protection from personal cross-examination from the respondent to any other witness who is particularly vulnerable.  For example, a friend of the affected family member who may feel intimidated by the prospect of being cross-examined by the respondent.

states that a protected witness must not be personally cross-examined by the respondent unless the protected person is an adult who has consented to being cross-examined and the court decides it would not have a harmful impact.  If the protected witness is an adult with a cognitive impairment, the court must also be satisfied that the protected witness is able to give valid consent and would be competent to give evidence.

outlines what the court must do where a respondent has been prohibited from personally cross-examining a protected witness to ensure that the respondent has the opportunity to obtain legal representation.
outlines how the respondent may be legally represented.

provides that if a respondent does not obtain legal representation the court must order Victoria Legal Aid to offer representation for the purpose of cross-examination. The purpose of this subclause is to ensure that respondents are not prevented from having a witness's evidence tested via cross-examination if the respondent cannot conduct the cross-examination himself or herself.

provides that Victoria Legal Aid must offer representation despite anything to the contrary in the Legal Aid Act 1978.  This means that Victoria Legal Aid must offer representation to respondents who would not otherwise meet the relevant eligibility test that applies to grants of legal aid.

provides that Victoria Legal Aid may apply conditions under section 27 of the Legal Aid Act 1978 to a grant of aid under this clause.  This means that Victoria Legal Aid may require a contribution to the cost of providing the representation, a payment towards any out-of-pocket expenses incurred by Victoria Legal Aid or a security over land or other property for the costs involved.

outlines the consequences for the respondent if legal representation is refused.  This subclause is intended to ensure that if the respondent does not avail themselves of legal representation to cross-examine protected witnesses about matters relevant to the application, the respondent and their witnesses will not be able to give evidence on those matters.

outlines how a protected witness who is the applicant may obtain legal representation.  This is to ensure that there is no disadvantage experienced by an applicant because the respondent has been provided with legal representation for the purpose of cross-examination if the applicant does not have representation.

notes that this clause applies if the respondent has been prohibited from personally cross-examining a protected witness and the applicant is not a police officer and does not have their own legal representation.  Police applicants are not covered by this clause as the police prosecutor will conduct these cases.

states that Victoria Legal Aid must provide legal representation for the applicant unless the protected witness objects to the provision of legal representation.  This is to ensure that an applicant is not forced to be legally represented if they do not wish to be represented.

states that representation must be provided by Victoria Legal Aid despite anything to the contrary in the Legal Aid Act 1978.  This means that Victoria Legal Aid must offer representation to protected witnesses who would not otherwise meet the means the eligibility test that applies to grants of legal aid.

provides that Victoria Legal Aid may apply conditions under section 27 of the Legal Aid Act 1978 to a grant of aid under this clause.  This means that Victoria Legal Aid may require a contribution to the cost of providing the representation, a payment towards any out-of-pocket expenses incurred by Victoria Legal Aid or a security over land or other property for the costs involved.

provides that the court may admit evidence about the dynamics and characteristics about family violence from experts to assist in decision-making.
Division 4—Making final orders
Division 4 outlines the circumstances in which the court can make a final order.

provides the court with a power to make a final order.  A final order may be made if the court has found that the respondent has on the balance of probabilities committed family violence, in accordance with the definition of family violence in clause 5, and is likely to do so again.  The court must find that the respondent is likely to commit family violence again as the purpose of the intervention order system is to protect family members from future violence.
(a) provides that if the court finds that the respondent has committed family violence against more than one family member, a final order may be made to protect each family member.

(b) provides that if all the parties consent or do not oppose the making of a family violence intervention order, the court has power to make an order for more than one affected family member.  Clause 78 further describes how consent orders are made.

outlines the power of the court to make a final order if there is a police application that the affected family member has not consented to.  In this case, the court may make a final order; however, the court is restricted as to the conditions it may impose on such an order.

provides that the final order may only include conditions that prohibit the respondent from committing family violence as defined by this Bill.  This may include prohibiting the respondent from assaulting, harassing, threatening or intimidating the protected person or damaging the protected person's property.  The court may also prohibit another person from engaging in conduct prohibited by the order and may revoke, cancel or suspend a firearms authority or weapons approval.

provides that a final order can be made without the protected person's consent on a police application with any conditions if the protected person is a child, has a guardian and the guardian has consented to the application or the person is cognitively impaired.  This subclause is to ensure that police have the power to take protective action for those who may not have the capacity to act in their own interests.

provides that the court can make final orders for those associated with the respondent or affected family member.  This clause has been included in response to a finding of the VLRC that associates of victims of family violence are often subject to violent and threatening behaviour from the perpetrator, particularly after an intervention order has been made. The VLRC also found that associates of respondents may be influenced by the respondent to commit violent and threatening behaviour on the respondent's behalf once an order has been made restricting the respondent's own behaviour.

gives the court a power to make a final order against an associate of the respondent where there is an order in place between the respondent and the protected person; the associate has subjected the protected person to behaviour that would come within the definition of family violence if they were family members and is likely to do so again.  An associate of a respondent is defined in clause 4 to mean a person who is so closely connected with the respondent that the respondent can influence their actions.

gives the court a power to make a final order to protect an associate of a protected person where the respondent has subjected the associate to behaviour that would be family violence if they were family members and is likely to do so again.  An associate of a protected person is defined in clause 4 to mean a person who provides the protected person with assistance or support.

provides that an application for an associated order may be heard at the same time as the original order.  This is to ensure efficiency in the court process and reduce the need for multiple court appearances by those affected and their witnesses. This subclause also provides that an associated order is not affected if the original order is varied, extended, revoked or otherwise ends.  This is because once an associated order is made, all other procedures under the Bill apply to the associated order as if it were a final order.  If the parties to the associated order wish to have the order varied, revoked or extended, the procedures under Division 8 of Part 4 will apply.

provides that an associate of a protected person can apply for an order, or an application can be made by any of those who can apply under clause 45 for an order.  This means, for example, that a police officer can apply for an order to protect an associate of an affected family member.
provides definitions of associated final order and original final order for the purpose of this clause.

provides the court with a power to make a final order to protect a child if the parties have not made an application on behalf of the child.  This is to ensure that children receive the protection of a final order if they have been subjected to family violence and the applicant has not included them in the application. This provision ensures that the court has an obligation to consider the needs of any children involved in a family violence situation that is before the court and therefore provides additional protection for children.

provides that before making any final order, the court must consider whether there are any children who are family members of the affected family member or respondent who have been subjected to family violence.  Under clause 5, being subjected to family violence includes where a respondent has caused a child to hear, witness or otherwise be exposed to the effects of family violence.

provides that if a court is satisfied that a child has been subjected to family violence and is likely to again be subjected to family violence, the court can make an order to protect the child.  If the need for protection is substantially the same as that of the affected family member, the child can be included on the final order as a protected person with the affected family member.  If it is not, the court can make a separate final order on behalf of the child, which will include different conditions to those included on the order for the affected family member.
outlines the circumstances in which a court can make a final order by consent.

provides that the court can make a final order without being satisfied that there are grounds for making the order if the parties have consented to or do not oppose the making of the final order.  The respondent does not need to admit any of the allegations made in the application in order to consent or not oppose the order being made.  This is to ensure that where the respondent is willing to have their behaviour constrained by the conditions of an order, the protected person does not need to go through a full court hearing.

provides an exception to clause 78(1) if the respondent is a child.  In this case, the court must be satisfied that there are grounds to make the order.  This clause has been included to provide additional protection to child respondents. Child respondents may consent or not oppose the making of an order without fully appreciating the consequences.  Therefore, in these cases, the court must be satisfied that the respondent child has committed family violence before making a final order against the child.  The length of any order made against a child respondent is limited, by clause 98, to 12 months unless there are exceptional circumstances.

provides that if an affected person's parent or guardian has consented to the making of an application, that parent or guardian is to be treated as a party for the purposes of consenting to or not opposing the making of an order.

provides that despite clause 78(1), the court may conduct a hearing if it believes it is in the interests of justice to do so.  An example may be if the court believes that the respondent does not fully understand the implications of not opposing the making of an order.  This may include the situation of a cross-application, where both parties have applied for an order against each other.  The VLRC found that victims of family violence will often consent to an order being made against them in order to receive the protection of an order made against the perpetrator.  This may be a situation where the court believes it is in the interests of justice to conduct a hearing.

states that a court may refuse to make a final order that the parties have consented to or have not opposed if the court believes it may pose a risk to the safety of one of the parties or a child of either of the parties.  An example may include if a perpetrator of violence has applied for an order against the victim.

provides that the court must consider whether there are any children of either of the parties that require the protection of an order, according to clause 77, regardless of whether the court decides to make an order under clause 78(1). This is to ensure that any children involved continue to receive the protection of an order where this is necessary even if other parties consent to or do not oppose a family violence intervention order being made.
Division 5—Conditions of family violence intervention orders Division 5 provides the types of conditions that may be included in an order to restrict the respondent's behaviour.  However, an order may include any condition the court thinks is necessary or desirable in the circumstances and the court is not limited by the list of types of conditions set out in clause 81. The court must consider the safety of the protected person as paramount when deciding what conditions to include.
provides a definition of residence for the purpose of this Division.

provides that the safety of the affected family member and any children involved must be the paramount consideration in determining the conditions that will be included in the family violence intervention order.  This clause has been included to guide the court as to what the most important consideration is when deciding on conditions for an order.
outlines the types of conditions that may be included in a family violence intervention order.

provides that the court can include any condition that appears necessary or desirable in the circumstances of the case.  This means that the court is not constrained by the examples of conditions listed in clause 81(2).

includes a list of conditions that may be included on a family violence intervention order.  These conditions have been specifically outlined because they are those most commonly included in intervention orders.  Clause 81(2)(a) reflects the new definition of family violence in the Bill.  The actual conditions which a court may add to a family violence intervention order may be more specific, for example, "the respondent must not assault, harass or intimidate the protected family member".  The terms of the conditions are a matter for the court to determine in every case.
includes an obligation on the court to consider whether the respondent should be excluded from the residence as a condition of the family violence intervention order.

provides that if a court makes a family violence intervention order, it must consider whether to include a condition that excludes the respondent from the residence. This is to ensure that the court considers this issue in every hearing, not only where an applicant has requested such a condition.

outlines what the court must consider when deciding whether to exclude the respondent.  These factors have been included to emphasise the importance of those who have experienced family violence being able to remain in the home and to minimise disruption to social networks or supports if a protected person is required to leave their home.

clarifies that this clause applies regardless of any legal or equitable rights in the residence.  This means, for example, that the court may exclude the respondent where the respondent is the owner of the property.  A court may also exclude a respondent from a rental property where the tenancy agreement is held by the respondent.  In this situation, the protected person may apply under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to have the tenancy agreement terminated and a new agreement made with the protected person (see Division 11 of

nodes.heading: Part 16—Amendments to the Residential Tenancies' Act 1997).
nodes.text: Part 16—Amendments to the Residential Tenancies' Act 1997).

provides that an exclusion condition against an adult respondent must be included in the family violence intervention order if the court has determined this is appropriate, unless the protected person objects.  This is to ensure that the protected person has an opportunity to inform the court of their wishes.  For example, the protected person may wish to relocate to premises the respondent is not aware of rather than remain in the residence.
outlines considerations where the court is considering excluding a child from the residence.
states that this clause applies if a family violence intervention order is being made against a child respondent.

provides additional matters for the court to consider if the respondent is a child.  This is to ensure that the competing interests of the child in remaining in the residence are taken into account by the court.

provides that if a court is considering excluding a child from the residence, it should do so only if it is satisfied that the child will have appropriate alternative accommodation, care and supervision.  This is to ensure that a respondent child will be appropriately cared for if excluded from their current residence by the family violence intervention order.  This requirement is despite the requirement in clause 80 for the safety of the affected family member and any children subjected to family violence to be the paramount consideration.

provides that if the respondent is an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child, the court must consider under clause 83(3) how the child can maintain the child's culture and identity.  This is based on the Aboriginal child placement principle from section 13 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

provides that if a court makes an exclusion condition in a family violence intervention order against a child respondent, then the court must notify the Secretary of the Department of Human Services (DHS) that the order has been made.  This will allow DHS to decide whether the child or family require any further assistance or whether protective action under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 is required.

provides that if the court requires information, the court may ask the Secretary of DHS to provide a report about the care, supervision and accommodation options available to the child if the child was excluded from their home.

provides that the Secretary of DHS must give the report within a prescribed time.  If the child is under the age of 17 years, the request for a report by the court will be treated by DHS as though it were a report about a significant concern for the wellbeing of a child under section 28 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

outlines how the court may obtain a new address for the service of documents on the respondent if the respondent is excluded from the residence.  This is to ensure that police officers have an improved prospect of locating the respondent to serve any future court documents.  For example, if the protected person applies to have a final order extended or varied, this application will need to be served on the respondent before the application can be heard.

provides that, if an exclusion condition has been made, the court must ask the respondent for an address for service and inform the respondent that if police cannot locate the respondent they may apply for information from public sector organisations, in accordance with clause 207.
provides that a respondent may provide an email address for service.  However, an email address will not be able to be used for documents requiring personal service.

provides that the respondent is not obliged to comply with the request to provide an address.  The intention is to encourage the respondent to give an address, not to mandate a requirement to give an address for service.

provides that an address provided by the respondent is not valid for service if the person living at the address advises the court that they do not consent to their address being used for service.  This is to protect the privacy of third parties who do not want their address being used as the address at which to serve any documents upon the respondent.
provides further details about conditions related to personal property that may be made under clause 81.

provides that an order may include a condition directing the respondent to return personal property belonging to the protected person or the protected person's family, or the protected person and respondent jointly if the property will enable the protected person's everyday life to continue with as little disruption as possible.  This clause may apply if the protected person has left the residence and requires basic personal property such as clothes, cooking equipment, a car, bicycle, medicine or children's possessions.

provides that if an exclusion condition is included on the order the court may include a condition stating that furniture and appliances necessary to the normal running of the home must remain in the home and the respondent can return to the residence (under certain conditions) to obtain any personal property that is not required to be kept in the residence.  This is to ensure that if a protected person is remaining in the residence, the respondent cannot remove necessary furniture and appliances, but will have the opportunity to remove their own personal property.

notes that any condition made under clause 86 is subject to any other order made by the Family Court or other court or tribunal with jurisdiction over property disputes.  This is to ensure that property disputes can be resolved in the appropriate jurisdiction and any condition imposed by a family violence intervention order applies in the absence of, or prior to, any determination of the property rights of the parties.

provides that any condition included under clause 86 does not affect the property ownership rights of the parties.  For example, if the court orders that the respondent's refrigerator is to remain in the residence under an exclusion condition, the respondent will still own the refrigerator and the Family Court will be able to take this into account in a division of property conducted during divorce proceedings.

provides that if the court decides to make a family violence intervention order and the protected person or respondent is the parent of a child, then the court is required to enquire whether there are any relevant Family Law Act orders in place or child protection orders made under section 515(1) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 on foot.

provides that if the court discovers, on enquiry, there are relevant Family Law Act (FLA) orders (as defined in this Bill) on foot and the Family Law Act orders and family violence intervention order would be inconsistent, then the court must to the extent of its powers under section 68R of the Family Law Act revive, vary, discharge or suspend the Family Law Act order.  This provision of the Bill does not set out the test that the court must apply.  The extent of the court's power, and circumstances when a magistrate may revive, vary, discharge or suspend the Family Law Act order, are set out in section 68R of the Family Law Act.

provides that if the court decides to make a family violence intervention order the court must decide if it will jeopardise the safety of the protected person or child for the child to have continuing contact with the respondent.

provides that when making this assessment, the fact that the respondent has not previously used violence against the child is not in itself sufficient reason to conclude that the child's safety is not at risk.  For example, there may be evidence of violence against others or against animals which would cause the court to consider that the child may be at risk from the respondent.

provides that if the court is satisfied that there are no Family Law Act orders on foot and the court is satisfied that the protected person's and the child's safety would not be jeopardised by the respondent having contact with the child, then the court must prescribe conditions making these negotiations between the protected person and the respondent on child contact as safe as possible for the protected person.  The court must also provide that the arrangements agreed by the parties must be recorded in writing.  This may include a letter, email or text message between the parties.  Not only will this minimise the risk of confusion about the terms of the contact agreed by the parties, but it will also mean that the protected person's safety will be considered when deciding how these arrangements will be negotiated.
provides that the court must prohibit a child's contact with a respondent under an order if the court decides such contact poses a risk to the protected person's or child's safety.

provides that if the court intends to make a family violence intervention order the court must enquire as to whether the respondent holds a firearms authority (as defined by this Bill), is a person who enjoys a weapons exemption (as defined by this Bill) or holds a weapons approval (as defined by this Bill).

provides that if the court makes an interim order it can suspend a respondent's firearms authority or weapons approval or suspend the application of a general weapons exemption to the respondent.  Clause 95(b) provides that if the court makes a final order it may include conditions which cancel the respondent's firearm authority, revoke the respondent's weapons approval or revoke the application of a general weapons exemption to the respondent. Division 6—Explanation of final order
outlines the court's obligation to explain a final order that it makes.
outlines matters that must be explained to the protected person and the respondent if either are before the court, including orders about contact with children.
provides that the explanation under clause 96(1) must be a clear oral explanation.

provides that the court must give the respondent and the protected person a written notice containing prescribed information.  This is to ensure that those affected by the order receive clear written information about the nature and consequences of the order that has been made.

provides that a failure to give an explanation in accordance with this clause does not affect the validity of the order.  This is to ensure that a procedural failure does not undermine the protective intent of the order.
Division 7—Duration of final order
Division 7 includes factors for the court to consider when deciding how long an order should last.
provides that the court may specify a period that an order will remain in force.

provides factors for the court to take into account when deciding on the length of an order.  These factors are based on a finding by the VLRC that under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 there was wide variation in the length of orders made and nothing to guide the court when making this decision.
also allows the court to have regard to any matters raised by the respondent that are relevant to the period of the order.

states that if the respondent is a child, the order should not last for longer than 12 months unless there are exceptional circumstances.  This is to ensure that orders made against young people are limited in duration.

provides that an order remains in force for the period specified in the order or, if no period is specified, until it is revoked by the court or set aside on appeal.  This means that an order without a specified duration can operate indefinitely. Division 8—Variation, revocation and extension of family violence intervention orders
Division 8 outlines how an order may be varied, revoked or extended. It includes who may make an application for a change to an order and what the court must consider when hearing such an application.
Subdivision 1—Variation and revocation of family violence intervention orders
provides the court with a power to vary or revoke a family violence intervention order.

provides that a court may vary or revoke an order on an application made by a person specified in clause 108 or on its own initiative if the order has been made on its own initiative to protect a child.

outlines factors for the court to consider when deciding whether to vary or revoke an order.  These factors are intended to ensure that the safety of the protected person is adequately considered before a change is made to the order.

provides that the court may vary an order rather than revoke it on an application for an order to be revoked. For example, a court may decide to remove an exclusion condition from the order rather than revoke all conditions in order to maintain some level of protection for the protected person.

provides that a court may make an interim variation.  This will enable a court to make urgent variations to a family violence intervention order, for example, before the respondent has necessarily been served with the application for variation. An interim variation may be particularly useful if there is a family violence intervention order in place without an exclusion condition and a violent incident occurs after hours necessitating the exclusion of the respondent.  In these cases, the application for variation is treated in the same procedural manner as an application for an interim family violence intervention order.
provides additional protection where the court is considering varying or revoking an order.

provides that the court must consider the needs of any other person protected by the order, aside from the applicant for the variation or revocation.  The court must also consider whether any persons have become members of the respondent's or protected person's family and whether any relevant Family Law Act orders have been made since the original order was made.

provides that the court may refuse an application, or make a different variation to the variation sought, if it is necessary to ensure the safety of another person protected by the order.  This is to ensure that another person protected by the order does not have their protection removed due to an application for a variation or revocation made by another person.

provides that if there is a child who has a continuing need for the protection provided by an order, and there is an application to vary or revoke that order, the court may make a new order for the child or vary the existing order to ensure the continued protection of the child.

provides that if a child has become a member of the respondent's or protected person's family since the family violence intervention order was made and that child meets the grounds for an order, the court can include the child on the protected person's order or make a separate order to protect the child.

provides that if there is a family violence intervention order which has been made or varied under clause 103 or 104 and future variations or orders are sought (or considered by a court) under clause 100, a reference in that clause to a court making an original order of its own motion under clause 77(2) will be taken to mean a court making a variation or order under clause 103 or 104.
Subdivision 2—Extension of final order
provides the court with a power to extend a final order.
provides that a court may extend an order on an application made by a person specified in clause 108 or on its own initiative if the order has been made on its own initiative to protect a child.
provides the grounds that must be satisfied for a court to extend an order.  These grounds are provided to ensure that the protection of an order is still necessary before an extension is granted.

clarifies that it is not necessary to show that the respondent has committed family violence against the protected person while the order was in force to obtain an extension. This is to ensure that an extension of an order is not refused merely because a respondent has complied with the conditions of the order.
provides that an order can be extended in the interim, before a respondent has been informed of the application.

provides that if a person applies to extend a final order and the respondent has not been served with the application, the court may make an interim order extending the final order for up to 28 days.
