This is to ensure that there is no gap in protection if a person applies for an extension close to the expiry date of the order while the respondent is located for service and a hearing date is set.
provides that an interim order made under clause 107(1) may be extended if it has not been possible to serve the respondent (for example if they have not been located for service).

provides that the interim order made under clause 107(1) must be served on the respondent with the application for an extension.  This is to ensure that the respondent is made aware that the final order is continuing in force beyond the original expiry date.
Subdivision 3—Application to vary, revoke or extend family violence intervention order

sets out who may make an application to vary, revoke or extend a family violence intervention order.  This includes all of those who may apply for a family violence intervention order under clause 45, including those who were not a party to the original proceedings.  For example, a police officer may apply for a variation where the original application was brought by the protected person or another police officer.
outlines the circumstances in which a respondent can apply for a variation or revocation of an order.
provides that the respondent may only apply if the court has given leave.

states that the court may only grant leave if the court is satisfied that there has been a change of circumstances since the order has been made and the change of circumstances may justify a variation or revocation of the order.  This is to ensure that respondents cannot use the variation and revocation proceedings to further harass the protected person with baseless applications.
outlines the circumstances in which a police officer can apply for a variation or extension of an order.
provides that a police application may be made without the consent of the protected person.

provides that if the protected person has not consented to the application, a variation can still be made on a police application but only to include limited conditions and cannot remove any conditions.  This is consistent with clause 75 which provides that an order can only include limited conditions if it is made on a police application without the consent of the affected family member.

provides that a police application can be made without the consent of the protected person if the person is a child, has a cognitive impairment or has a guardian and the guardian has consented to the application.  This clause is to ensure that police have the power to take protective action for those who may not have the capacity to act in their own interests.

clarifies that a police officer does not have an obligation to bring an application for variation or extension if requested by a person protected by an order.  This is to ensure that police officers do not become de facto legal representation for all variation and extension hearings.

provides that certain applications must be made with written consent of the protected person, a child's parent or the person's guardian.  This is to ensure that applications to vary, revoke or extend orders are not able to proceed if the protected person or persons with the responsibility to protect a child or vulnerable party do not consent (unless it is the police officer's application).

provides that if a protected person has a guardian and the guardian makes an application under this Part, the person may be heard separately if they object to the application.  This is similar to the effect of clause 64, to ensure that persons with a guardian can inform the court if they object to protective measures being taken on their behalf by their guardian.
Subdivision 4—Service of applications for variations, revocations or extensions of orders

outlines who must be served with an application made under this Division, to ensure that all relevant persons are aware of the application. Division 9—Appeals and rehearings
Subdivision 1—Appeals to County Court and Supreme Court
provides for who may appeal against the making of a family violence intervention order or a refusal to make such an order.
provides limitations on who may appeal—
only the respondent to a counselling order can appeal that order;

that if the protected person did not apply for the original family violence intervention order and the applicant goes on to appeal the decision, the protected person or those with responsibility for the protected person are required to consent to the appeal;
that a person appealing against a decision to declare them vexatious, must appeal under clause 195, not this provision;
that a vexatious litigant must be granted leave under clause 96 before they can appeal a decision on an application under this Bill.

provides that an appeal under this Subdivision must be made to the County Court, unless the appeal relates to a decision by the President of the Children's Court in which case the appeal must be made to the Trial Division of the Supreme Court.
provides for what a notice to appeal must include, where it must be filed and on whom it must be served.
provides that an appeal against a decision does not operate as a stay of the Magistrates' Court or Children's Court decision, unless it is a counselling order.
allows a court to make an order staying the original decision pending the determination of the appeal.
provides that the court may impose bail conditions on an appellant to ensure the safety of a protected person or to ensure a party's attendance at the appeal.

provides that if the applicant for a family violence intervention order was not the protected person and that applicant is appealing a decision, the appeal cannot proceed unless the protected person or those with responsibility for the protected person (such as a parent or guardian) consents to the appeal. This is to ensure that a protected person or a person with the responsibility for a protected person can decide what matters are appealed on their behalf or on behalf of those for whom they have responsibility.
provides that an appeal against a decision of the original court is by way of a rehearing and sets out the powers of an appeal court in relation to the original decision.
provides that there is no appeal against a decision of the County or Supreme Court determining an appeal from a Magistrates' Court or Children's Court.

provides that if an appeal is being heard then the provisions of the Bill, and the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 or Children Youth and Families Act 2005 apply in the appeal hearing. As an appeal is by way of rehearing (see clause 119), this is particularly relevant to how proceedings may be conducted, how evidence may be given, prohibitions on personal cross-examination of a protected witness and prohibitions on publication of identifying information.
Subdivision 2—Rehearings

provides for a person to seek a rehearing of an application if an order has been made and that person was not served with the application, nor made aware of it under an order for substituted service.  An application for a rehearing does not operate as a stay on the final order or order declaring a person to be vexatious.
Division 10—Contravention of family violence intervention order Division 10 provides that contravening a condition of an order is a criminal offence.
states that contravening an order is a criminal offence.  This is to ensure that the conditions of the order can be enforced.
provides that a person must have been served with a copy of the order or had an explanation of the order given in accordance with clause 57 or 96.

provides that contravening the order is an offence, punishable by Level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum) or level 7 fine (240 penalty units maximum).  This penalty level was informed by a report of the Sentencing Advisory Council, Report on Maximum Penalties for Breaches of Intervention Orders.

provides that, if the person was the respondent for the order and a family violence safety notice when the offence was committed, it is a defence if the person's conduct did not contravene the family violence safety notice.

provides that a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant if the officer believes on reasonable grounds that the person has contravened a family violence intervention order. This power of arrest and detention without a warrant has been provided to provide further protection to the person protected by the order.  The Bail Act 1977 will apply in these circumstances.

provides that a person protected by an order cannot be guilty of aiding, abetting, counselling or procuring an offence of contravening a family violence intervention order or family violence safety notice.  This is to ensure that it is the respondent for the order who is held responsible for complying with the order, not the protected person.  The clause includes some common examples where a protected person may permit the respondent to act in contravention of the order to guide interpretation.

nodes.heading: PART 5—COUNSELLING ORDERS Division 1—Preliminary
nodes.text: PART 5—COUNSELLING ORDERS Division 1—Preliminary
defines the term legal practitioner for the purposes of the Part.

sets out the main object of the Part, which is to empower the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court to make orders to assess the eligibility of certain respondents for counselling and to require a respondent to attend counselling, where appropriate.

provides that the Part only applies in certain circumstances. Thus, it will only apply if the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court makes a final order against an adult respondent who resided, at the time of the family violence the subject of the order, within a particular geographic area. Division 2—Orders to assess eligibility for and to attend counselling
relates to the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court making orders for a respondent to a final order to be assessed for his or her eligibility for counselling.

provides that, if the Family Violence Court Division makes a final order and the requirements for the application of the Part are satisfied, it must make an order requiring the respondent to be assessed as to their eligibility for counselling.
provides limited exceptions to the requirement in clause 129(1).  The Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court is not required to make an order if—
the respondent is already the subject of a counselling order made under to clause 130; or

it is satisfied that there is no approved counselling that it is reasonably practicable for the respondent to attend or that, for any other reason, it is not appropriate in all the circumstances of the case.

The order to assess eligibility requires a person who is approved by the Secretary to the Department of Justice to give a report to the Family Violence Court Division, by a date specified in the order, on whether the respondent is eligible to attend counselling.  The counselling is that which is approved by the Secretary to the Department of Justice under clause 130.

provides that the report must assess the respondent as eligible to attend counselling unless the person making the report believes the respondent does not have the ability or capacity to participate in counselling.  That belief must be based on at least one of these factors—
the respondent's character, personal history or language skills;
any disabilities of the respondent;
any severe psychiatric or psychological conditions of the respondent;
any alcohol or other drug problems of the respondent;
any other matter the person preparing the report considers relevant.

creates a requirement that the time and place of interview be specified in the order for the eligibility interview. That time and place may be varied by the appropriate registrar of the Family Violence Court Division provided reasonable notice of that variation is given in writing to the respondent.
Clauses 129(5) and (6) provide that failure to attend the interview without reasonable excuse is an offence and the respondent will be liable to a fine not exceeding 10 penalty units.
provides for the making of counselling orders.

enables the Family Violence Court Division to order a respondent to a family violence intervention order to attend counselling if it receives a report under clause 129 and is satisfied that the respondent is eligible to attend counselling.

further provides that the Family Violence Court Division is not required to make the order to attend counselling if there is already an order in force for the respondent to attend counselling (for example, this may be as a result of an intervention order that relates to a different affected family member or protected person).
The Family Violence Court Division is not required to order the respondent to attend counselling if it is satisfied there is no counselling approved by the Secretary that is reasonably practicable for the respondent to attend (for example, where it is satisfied that the respondent is residing interstate).  Further, the Family Violence Court Division may decide not to order the respondent to attend counselling if it is satisfied that it is not appropriate to do so for any other reason.

requires the court to include in the order the time and place for the initial counselling session.  This may be varied by the appropriate registrar for the Family Violence Court Division providing that reasonable written notice is given to the respondent.  Orders to attend counselling must also require the counselling provider to give reasonable written notice to the respondent of the time and place of subsequent counselling sessions.
provides that it is an offence to fail to attend counselling without a reasonable excuse and the respondent will be liable to a penalty not exceeding 10 penalty units.
provides that a respondent may only be prosecuted once for an offence against subclause (4), irrespective of how many counselling sessions the respondent does not attend.
sets out the effect of an appeal against a final order.

stays the operation of an order to attend an eligibility interview or counselling if an appeal is lodged against a family violence intervention order in respect of the respondent and the operation of the whole of the intervention order is stayed.  If the final order ceases to be in force as a result of the appeal, the counselling order will also cease to be in force. This clause is subject to the appellate court making a contrary order.

provides that a counselling order will not otherwise cease to be in force merely because the final order against the respondent ceases to be in force.
Division 3—Procedures relating to counselling orders
Division 3 outlines procedures relating to counselling orders.

requires the appropriate registrar of the Family Violence Court Division to serve written notice of a hearing in respect of an order to attend an eligibility interview or counselling on the respondent.  Because some respondents will already be before the court following the making of an intervention order, the provision allows that in these circumstances notice to the respondent of the hearing for making (varying or revoking) a counselling order is not required.
Under clause 132(4), the requirement to give notice of a hearing does not apply to a variation of the time or place at which an interview under clause 129(4), or counselling under clause 130(3), is to be conducted.

sets out the regime for the Secretary to the Department of Justice to approve people to assess eligibility for counselling and to approve counselling.
Clauses 133(1) and (2) enable the Secretary to approve persons to conduct interviews and prepare reports concerning eligibility for counselling, and for approval of counselling, for the purposes of orders under Part 5.  The Secretary must consider the person to have appropriate experience and qualifications.

allows the Family Violence Court Division to have access to a list of persons to conduct eligibility interviews and persons or bodies to provide counselling, since the court will be making orders for persons to attend upon these persons or bodies.

provides that a person who gives a report to the Family Violence Court Division as to eligibility of a respondent for counselling may be required to attend court to give evidence. The respondent or the court may require that person's attendance.  The respondent may cross-examine this person on the contents of the report.

sets limits on the extent to which the Family Violence Court Division may take into account a report on eligibility of a respondent that is disputed by the respondent.  It must not take the disputed matter into consideration unless it is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the matter is true.
The court cannot take the disputed report, or the disputed part of the report, into consideration if the person who prepared the report fails to attend the hearing despite having been required to do so under clause 134, unless the respondent consents to the report, or the disputed part of the report, being taken into account.

requires the Family Violence Court Division to explain orders to attend an eligibility interview or counselling when the respondent is before the court.  Such an explanation must include the following matters—
the purpose, terms and effect of the proposed order; and
the consequences that may follow if the respondent fails to comply with the terms of the proposed order; and
the ways in which the proposed order may be varied or revoked.
sets out how orders to attend a counselling eligibility interview or counselling may be varied or revoked.

provides for the variation and revocation of orders to attend an eligibility interview and orders to attend counselling.  These orders may be varied or revoked if there is no counselling approved by the Secretary to the Department of Justice that it is reasonably practicable for the respondent to attend.  An order to attend counselling may also be varied or revoked if there has been a significant change in circumstances in which the order was made that significantly impacts upon the respondent's ability or capacity to participate in counselling.

provides that the respondent may apply for a variation or revocation of an order to attend an eligibility interview or an order to attend counselling.  A person required to undertake the eligibility interview and prepare a report may apply for a variation or revocation of an order to attend an eligibility interview.  The counselling provider may apply for a variation or revocation of an order to attend counselling.

provides that the appropriate registrar of the Family Violence Court Division must cause a copy of an application to revoke or vary an order to attend an eligibility interview or counselling to be served on the person authorised to undertake the interview and report, or the person or body authorised to provide counselling, as the case may be.  If the respondent is not the applicant for the variation or revocation, the appropriate registrar must cause a copy of the application to be served on the respondent.

provides for service of orders to attend an eligibility interview or counselling, and for service of orders for their revocation or variation.  After arranging for the orders to be drawn up and filed in the Family Violence Court Division, the registrar must arrange for a copy of the order to be served on the respondent as soon as practicable, and not later than 10 days, after it is made.

(c) provides that in the case of an order to attend an eligibility interview or its variation or revocation, the appropriate registrar must give a copy to the person specified in the order to conduct the eligibility interview and prepare the report for the court.  Similarly, the registrar must give a copy of an order to attend counselling, or its revocation or variation, to the person or body specified in the order to conduct the counselling.

requires the appropriate registrar to serve an eligibility report or a certificate of non-attendance at counselling (as provided for under clause 139) on the respondent no later than 10 days after the Family Violence Court Division receives it.
Division 4—Other matters
Division 4 sets out other matters relating to counselling orders.

provides that if a respondent fails to attend an eligibility interview or counselling as ordered (failure to attend is further defined in clauses 129 and 130), the person who would have performed the interview or the person or body that would have provided the counselling may give the court a certificate setting out the details of the failure to attend.  In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the certificate is proof of the facts contained in it.  This certificate will enable the court to deal with the matter without requiring the person who provided the certificate to attend court to give evidence as to the failure to attend an eligibility interview or counselling, unless the certificate is disputed.

protects the privacy of respondents who attend an eligibility interview as ordered under clause 129.  The person who conducts the interview or prepares the report for the court is restricted from making a disclosure of information obtained from these activities other than—
a disclosure by, or authorised by, the respondent the subject of the report;
a disclosure to a legal practitioner representing a party in a proceeding under the Bill;

a disclosure authorised by the Family Violence Court Division as necessary for the purposes of Part 5 or of proceedings for or with respect to a contravention of an order under Part 5 (including any offence constituted by such a contravention);
a disclosure required, authorised or permitted by law or a court;
certain disclosures authorised by the Health Records Act 2001;
a disclosure that does not identify the respondent or from which the respondent's identity cannot reasonably be ascertained.

protects the privacy of respondents ordered to attend counselling under clause 130.  The person or body conducting the counselling is restricted from making a disclosure of information obtained during the course of the counselling other than—
a disclosure by, or authorised by, the respondent the subject of the report;
a disclosure to a legal practitioner representing a party in a proceeding under the Bill;

a disclosure authorised by the Family Violence Court Division as necessary for the purposes of Part 5 or of proceedings for or with respect to a contravention of an order under Part 5 (including any offence constituted by such a contravention);
a disclosure required, authorised or permitted by law or a court;
certain disclosures authorised by the Health Records Act 2001;
a disclosure that does not identify the respondent or from which the respondent's identity cannot reasonably be ascertained.

protects the privacy of respondents by restricting the use any court may make of information that the Family Violence Court Division obtains from a report as to eligibility to attend counselling or in respect of attendance at counselling.

clarifies that the Bill allows for the collection of health information within the bounds provided in the Health Records Act 2001.  A person or body that conducts an interview or prepares a report as to eligibility to attend counselling, or a person or body who provides counselling, is authorised to collect health information to the extent that it is necessary for those activities.

empowers the Secretary to the Department of Justice to delegate (by instrument), to any person employed under Part 3 of the Public Administration Act 2004, any power the Secretary has under this Division, except the power of delegation.

nodes.heading: PART 6—JURISDICTION OF COURTS AND PROCEEDINGS Division 1—Jurisdiction of courts
nodes.text: PART 6—JURISDICTION OF COURTS AND PROCEEDINGS Division 1—Jurisdiction of courts
Division 1 outlines the jurisdiction of the courts in relation to family violence intervention orders, in particular the jurisdiction of the Magistrates' Court and the Children's Court.
sets out a definition of the Children's Court and the Magistrates' Court.
outlines the jurisdiction if the affected family member, protected person or respondent is a child.
provides that both the Magistrates' Court and the Children's Court have jurisdiction if this is the case.

provides that if the respondent is a child the matter should be heard in the Children's Court if practicable. This is to ensure that children who are respondents have access to the additional services and supports available through the Children's Court when an application is made against them.
provides the Children's Court with jurisdiction to deal with related applications.
outlines the circumstances that this clause applies to.  That is, if an application involves a child and there is a related application between adults.

states that in these circumstances the Children's Court also has jurisdiction over the related application.  This has been provided in response to a finding by the VLRC that victims are sometimes required to attend two separate hearings to obtain protection for themselves and their children—one in the Magistrates' Court and one in the Children's Court.  The effect of this clause is that if the Children's Court has jurisdiction by virtue of a protected person, affected person or respondent being a child then any related application between two adults can be heard by the Children's Court, therefore reducing the need for multiple court appearances and hearings.
provides definitions for this clause, including that a related application is one made on the grounds of the same or similar circumstances.
outlines how an application may be transferred between courts.
provides that the Magistrates' Court may transfer an application under this Bill to the Children's Court if it considers it appropriate in the circumstances.
provides that the Children's Court may transfer an application under this Bill to the Magistrates' Court if it considers it appropriate in the circumstances.

provides the Magistrates' Court and the Children's Court with a power to vary, revoke or extend any order made under this Bill. This is to ensure that parties do not need to return to the same court to have any changes made to the order.

provides that even if a decision has been confirmed or varied on appeal, a Magistrates' Court or Children's Court may vary or revoke the decision of the superior court if a party applies for a variation or revocation but only if the court is satisfied there are new facts or circumstances relevant to the order.
Division 2—Provisions about proceedings under this Act

restricts the presence of children in proceedings under the Bill. This is to reduce the likelihood of children being traumatised by involvement in the court process and being drawn into conflict between their parents.

outlines which children must not be present during proceedings.  This is aimed at ensuring no children who are related to the family members involved are present, but that a child who is not related (for example, a neighbour who has witnessed an incident of family violence) may be present. This subclause makes clear that this restriction also applies to proceedings for offences under this Bill as well as for civil proceedings.
provides that a child who is a respondent or defendant in criminal proceedings can be present, as well as any child that the court allows to be present.

outlines what the court must consider when deciding whether to allow a child to be present.  This is to ensure that the court considers the potential harmful effect of allowing the child to be present.
provides that the court can adjourn any proceeding to allow the parties to obtain legal advice.

provides that if a police officer makes an application, the officer can be represented by another police officer or another person nominated by the Chief Commissioner.  This is to ensure that a police officer who attends a family violence incident does not need to be the officer who makes the application in court. A police prosecutor will usually make the application.

outlines the requirements for certifying documents under the Bill and creates an offence of falsely certifying a document. The maximum penalty for a contravention is 120 penalty units. The certifying process can be used by police officers or court registrars, to certify service of documents, completing family violence safety notices particularly if issued by telephone, fax or other means of electronic communication and for completing applications for family violence intervention orders.  It is designed to be quicker and more efficient than swearing or affirming a document which requires the presence of two persons.
outlines the costs provisions that apply under the Bill.
provides that each party must bear their own costs.

provides that a party to vexatious litigant proceedings under Part 11 must bear the cost of proceedings if that party is declared a vexatious litigant, except for any costs of the Attorney-General.  This is to ensure that a person dealing with a vexatious litigant by having the person declared vexatious by the court is not financially disadvantaged.  If the party is not declared vexatious, then each party bears their own costs.

provides exceptions to the rules in subclauses (1) and (2).  The court may make an order about costs if there are exceptional circumstances or if the application was vexatious, frivolous or made in bad faith.

clarifies that the mere fact that an application was made and then withdrawn is not exceptional and does not necessarily amount to a vexatious or frivolous application. This is to ensure, for example, that victims of family violence who change their mind about applying for an order are not penalised by the court making a costs order against them.

states that the court may adjourn proceedings where the person who it is considering making a costs order against is not present in court.  This is to ensure that the person has an opportunity to be heard by the court before an order is made given that this is usually a jurisdiction where parties bear their own costs.

clarifies that a family violence intervention order can be made if there are also criminal proceedings for the same conduct.  This is because a family violence intervention order is a civil remedy to protect those experiencing violence rather than a criminal sanction.

provides that if a family violence intervention order is made against an employed carer or carer who is engaged by an auspicing agency, the court must inform the employer or organisation auspicing the care arrangement that the order has been made.  This is to ensure that appropriate steps can be taken to change the care arrangements for the protected person and to consider whether any other responses are necessary.

nodes.heading: PART 7—ENFORCEMENT POWERS
nodes.text: PART 7—ENFORCEMENT POWERS

provides police officers with a power to enter and search premises for a person in a number of circumstances.  This power is in addition to any powers of entry and search under the Crimes Act 1958, any other Act or common law search powers. This search power is included to ensure that police officers have adequate powers to act to protect a person who is experiencing family violence, including if the family violence is not necessarily a crime.

creates an offence for a failure to surrender firearms or weapons when directed to do so by police.  It provides that if a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order has been made or if a police officer is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there are grounds for making either a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order and the police officer is aware that a person has firearms, a firearm authority (as defined by this Bill), ammunition or weapon (as defined by this Bill) in their possession the police officer may direct those items be surrendered.
specifies that surrender may be required immediately or directed to occur at a specified place and time within 48 hours.  If the surrender is not immediate, the direction must be in writing.

makes it an offence not to comply with such a direction without lawful excuse.  The maximum penalty for such a contravention is 60 penalty units in the case of a firearm and 30 penalty units in relation to any other item.

provides a power for police to search certain premises or vehicles without a warrant if an officer is aware or has reasonable grounds to suspect firearms or weapons are in the respondent's possession.
Clauses 159(1) and (2) provide that if—
a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order has been made; or
a police officer is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there are grounds for making either a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order; and
the police officer is aware that a person has firearms, a firearm authority (as defined by this Bill), ammunition or weapon (as defined by this Bill) in their possession; or
reasonably suspects this is the case—
then the police officer may enter and search without warrant any vehicle registered to the person or any premises at which the person—
resides;
has resided; or
committed or allegedly committed family violence.
provides reasonable force may be used by a police officer to effect such an entry.
provides for circumstances in which a search of third party premises or vehicle may be required.

provides that a police officer can only apply for such a search warrant if they intend to apply for either a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order or if either of these has already been made.  The police officer must also believe on reasonable grounds that—
a person is committing or about to commit an offence under this Bill; or

the person is in possession of a firearm, a firearms authority (as defined by this Bill), ammunition or a weapon (as defined by this Bill) at third party premises or vehicle (i.e. not where the person resides or has resided and not where the family violence was committed or alleged to have been committed).
gives a magistrate the power to issue a search warrant to search and seize evidence or a firearm, a firearms authority, ammunition or a weapon.

sets out the matters that must be set out in the issued warrant.
Clauses 160(4) and (5) provides that the procedural requirements for search warrants required in the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 and associate rules and regulations apply to the search warrant issued under this Bill.
provides the process that must be followed by the police when executing a search warrant.
provides that a police officer executing a search warrant must identify themselves and give an execution copy of the search warrant to the occupier of the premises.

provides that if a person does not surrender a firearm, firearms authority, ammunition or weapon when directed under clause 158 or if the police officer searches without a warrant under clause 159, a police officer must seize any firearms or firearms authority and may seize any ammunition or weapon.
provides for what happens to seized property under Part 7.

provides that if a person's firearm, firearms authority, ammunition or weapon is seized under the Bill and a final order is made then the seized firearm can be returned only if the respondent has successfully applied under section 189 of the Firearms Act 1996 to be deemed "not a prohibited person" and the firearm is not required as evidence for an offence and has not been ordered to be forfeited after a criminal proceeding. Otherwise, the firearm is to be, disposed of according to the final order or if the final order is silent on the issue, according to the Firearms Act 1996.
A seized weapon is to be returned to the owner if the person is declared not to be a prohibited person under the Firearms Act 1996 but otherwise must be forfeited to the Crown or disposed of as directed in the final order.
provides if an item seized under Part 7 is ordered to be disposed of by sale then proceeds of sale must be paid to the owner of the firearm.

provides for what should happen to seized items if no final order is made.
Under clause 165(2), if a person's firearm, firearms authority, ammunition or weapon is seized under Part 7, but then a final order is not made or no application is made for a family violence intervention order or family violence safety notice within a reasonable time, the seized items must be returned unless otherwise required to be forfeited under another Act or order.

nodes.heading: PART 8—RESTRICTION ON PUBLICATION OF PROCEEDINGS
nodes.text: PART 8—RESTRICTION ON PUBLICATION OF PROCEEDINGS

restricts the publication of proceedings in the Magistrates' Court in various circumstances.
If a child is involved in the proceedings, either as a party, a witness or a person the subject of an order, the clause prohibits publication of a report about the proceedings or an order that contains—
the locality of the court or any other particulars that are likely to lead to the identification of the particular venue of the court; or
any particulars likely to lead to the identification of the child or any other person involved in the proceedings, whether as a party, a witness or the subject of the order.
In any other proceeding in which a child is not involved, any reports of proceedings must not contain—
any particulars which are likely to lead to the identification of any person involved in the proceedings or who are the subject of the order, unless the court orders otherwise under clause 169; or
a picture of or including a person concerned in proceedings for a family violence intervention order, unless the court orders otherwise under clause 169.

The penalty for contravention of this clause is, in the case of a body corporate, a fine 500 penalty units and, in any other case, a fine of 100 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years.  This is to ensure the penalties are equivalent to similar provisions in section 534 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, which governs publication of proceedings in the Children's Court.
restricts the application of clause 166.  Therefore, clause 166 does not apply to—

a person who publishes, or who effects the publishing of, a report about the proceedings or the order if the publication does not identify the locality of a court or particulars likely to identify a venue of a court, or particulars of a person; or
the publication by the Attorney-General, under clause 198, of a copy of any order made under clauses 193 or 197.
sets out, for the purposes of clauses 166 and 167, a non-exhaustive list of particulars that are likely to lead to the identification of a person.  These include—
the person's name, title, pseudonym or alias;
the address of any premises at which the person lives or works, or the locality where those premises are situated;
the address of a school attended by the person or the locality where the school is situated;
the physical description or the style of dress of the person;
any employment or occupation engaged in, profession practised or calling pursued by, the person or any official or honorary position held by the person;

the relationship of the person to identified relatives of the person or the association of the person with identified friends or identified business, official or professional acquaintances of the person;
the recreational interests or the political, philosophical or religious beliefs or interests of the person;
any real or personal property in which the person has an interest or with which the person is associated.
provides the circumstances in which the court may allow the publication of particulars or a picture.  Thus, the court may make an order allowing such publication if it reasonably considers that—
it is in the public interest to allow the publication of the particulars or picture; and
it is just to allow the publication in the circumstances; and
for a picture, the picture is not of and does not include a child and will not be likely to lead to the identification of a child.

nodes.heading: PART 9—RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER ACTS
nodes.text: PART 9—RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER ACTS

provides that Part 5 of the Magistrates Court Act 1989 and any rules made in relation to Part 5 do not apply to proceedings under this Bill with the exception of sections 100(1)(d) and 109 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.  Section 100(1)(d) states that the court has jurisdiction to hear and determine "any cause of action if the Court is given jurisdiction to do so by or under any Act other than [the Magistrates' Court Act 1989]". Section 109 provides for appeals to the Supreme Court on questions of law.
This provision is designed to avoid confusion about whether proceedings under the Bill are civil proceedings and therefore subject to the legislation and rules which relate to civil proceedings in the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.  The Bill and any rules and regulations made under that Bill will govern proceedings under the Bill.

provides that if a court suspends, revokes or cancels a firearms authority as a condition of a family violence intervention order then whilst the respondent may appeal the terms of the order under this Bill, there can be no appeal under the Firearms Act 1996 against this decision and no application under section 189 of the Firearms Act 1996 in respect of the respondent's "prohibited person" status under the Firearms Act 1996.

clarifies that when the Children's Court exercises jurisdiction and makes decisions under the Bill it is not required to have regard to those principles set out in Part 1.2 of Chapter 1 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

provides that a family violence intervention order applies despite any child protection order under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.  This replicates the current law in the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and ensures that there is no confusion about what court order prevails in any situation.

, however, provides that if the Children's Court is hearing a child protection matter under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, it may vary or revoke a family violence intervention order to the extent it is inconsistent with a child protection order that it wishes to make under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

provides that if the Children's Court proposes to make a variation or revocation under clause 173(2), then this should be on an interim basis until all the parties who would be affected by such a variation or revocation can be given notice and be heard.

provides that if a family violence intervention order is made that is or may be inconsistent with a child protection order, the appropriate registrar of the court should notify the Secretary of DHS.  This will enable the Secretary of DHS to consider whether a new application should be made to the Children's Court under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005. If such an application is made, the Children's Court under clause 173 can vary or revoke the family violence intervention order to the extent of the inconsistency.

provides if a warrant is issued under clause 50 and a person is apprehended under that warrant and is granted bail, then the bail conditions prevail over any child protection order to the extent of any inconsistency while the bail conditions are in place.
clarifies the relationship between family violence intervention orders and orders made under the Family Law Act.

nodes.heading: PART 10—INTERSTATE AND NEW ZEALAND ORDERS Division 1—Interstate orders
nodes.text: PART 10—INTERSTATE AND NEW ZEALAND ORDERS Division 1—Interstate orders
provides for registration of corresponding interstate orders in the court.  Such orders are defined in clause 4.

provides for the people who must be notified of the registration of corresponding interstate orders.
Clauses 178(2) and (3) provide that a registrar may list the question of service for the court's determination.  The court may then order that a registered interstate order be served on the respondent but only if satisfied that disclosing the protected person's whereabouts in Victoria will not jeopardise the safety of a protected person or any children of the protected person.
provides that once registered in Victoria, an interstate order may be enforced as though it is a final order made under the Bill.

provides that if a registered interstate order is varied, extended or revoked in the State or Territory court is was made in after it is registered in Victoria, that variation, extension or revocation has no effect in Victoria.
provides that the court may vary, extend or revoke a corresponding interstate order that has been registered under clause 177.  Clause 181(2) lists who may make such an application.

provides that a variation, extension or revocation of a registered corresponding interstate order cannot be made unless notice has been given to the person against whom it is made and for whose protection it is made.

sets out who the court must notify if it varies, extends or revokes a registered corresponding interstate order.
Division 2—Corresponding New Zealand orders
provides that an appropriate registrar of a court may register a corresponding New Zealand order in the court.

sets out who the appropriate registrar must notify when the New Zealand order has been registered.  Clauses 185(2) and (3) provide that a registrar may list the question of service for the court's determination.  The court may then order that a registered corresponding New Zealand order be served on the respondent but only if satisfied that disclosing that the protected person is in Victoria will not jeopardise the safety of a protected person or any children of the protected person.
provides that a corresponding New Zealand order registered in Victoria has the same effect in Victoria as it does in New Zealand and may be enforced as though it is a final order under the Bill.

provides that if the corresponding New Zealand order is registered in Victoria but is then varied, extended or revoked by a court in New Zealand, the registered order is varied, extended or revoked accordingly.  The appropriate registrar of the Victorian court must then notify the Chief Commissioner of Police of the variation, extension or revocation.

nodes.heading: PART 11—VEXATIOUS LITIGANTS
nodes.text: PART 11—VEXATIOUS LITIGANTS

provides that the Chief Magistrate, Deputy Chief Magistrate or President of the Children's Court must hear vexatious litigant matters.  This is because the Magistrates' and Children's Court do not usually have the power to declare a person a vexatious litigant.

sets out who may apply for a vexatious litigant order. An application may be made by the Attorney-General or, with the leave of the court, a person against whom applications under this Bill or complaints under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 have been made.  The requirement for leave is to ensure that applications have merit and would not be an abuse of process before a person is summonsed to court for a vexatious litigant hearing.

provides that if the Attorney-General requests access to court documents, so that a decision can be made about whether to make a vexatious litigant application, the court may give a copy of the documents requested.

provides that if the Attorney-General makes an application to have a person declared a vexatious litigant, a copy of the application must be served on the person who would be protected by the vexatious litigant order.  This is to ensure that the person is aware of the application and may attend court for the hearing.

provides that the person proposed to be declared a vexatious litigant must have a copy of the application served on them. This is to ensure that the person is aware of the application and may attend court for the hearing.
sets out the power of the court to declare a person a vexatious litigant.

provides that a vexatious litigant order may be made if the court is satisfied that the person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable ground instituted proceedings under the Bill.  This reflects the test for a vexatious litigant order under the Supreme Court Act 1986. This provision is included to ensure that the procedures under the Bill cannot be misused as a form of harassment and to acknowledge that it would only be appropriate to limit a person's access to the court system if the person had demonstrably abused court processes in the past.

provides that a person who is declared a vexatious litigant cannot begin any proceedings under the Bill against the person protected by the order or their children without the leave of the court.  This is to ensure that the person declared a vexatious litigant can still use the provisions of the Bill, but must demonstrate that it would not be an abuse of process to do so before the person protected by the order is required to attend court for a hearing.
provides that a copy of the order declaring a person to be vexatious must be served on certain people.
provides that the order must be accompanied by the reasons that the court made the order.

states that when deciding whether to grant leave under clause 193 to allow a vexatious litigant to apply for a family violence intervention order, or variation, revocation or extension of such an order, the court may be constituted by any Magistrate and the hearing should occur as soon as practicable.  This is to ensure that a person declared a vexatious litigant does not experience a long delay as there may be grounds for an application under the Bill to be made.

outlines how a person may appeal against a vexatious litigant order.  The court to which a vexatious litigant appeals, may grant leave for the appeal if satisfied that there is evidence the appeal has merit and is not an abuse of process.  This is to ensure that a vexatious litigant does not use the appeal process to further harass a protected person.  If leave is granted, the appropriate registrar must serve notice of the hearing date on the vexatious litigant, the person protected by the order and if the Attorney-General was the original applicant, the Attorney-General.

outlines how a person who has been declared a vexatious litigant may bring an appeal against any other decision that has been made under the Bill.  The clause sets out who must be notified and what documents must be filed in which court if leave to appeal is granted.  The person protected by the order may be heard on the leave application.  The County Court or Supreme Court (if the appeal is from a decision of the President of the Children's Court) must consider all the circumstances of the case when deciding whether or not to grant leave, including the statement (see clause 193(4)) setting out a summary of the grounds for the order declaring the person to be a vexatious litigant.

provides that a vexatious litigant order may be varied, set aside or revoked.  A vexatious litigant may apply to have the order varied, set aside or revoked but can only do so with the leave of the court.  This is to ensure that the making of vexatious litigant orders can be reviewed, but, if the vexatious litigant applies, the court must be satisfied there is merit in the application and it is not an abuse of process.

provides that the Attorney-General must publish a copy of any vexatious litigant order made (and any variations or revocations) in the Government Gazette, without the name of the person who is protected by the vexatious litigant order.  This requirement recognises the serious consequences of making a vexatious litigant order and ensures that there is a public record of an order that limits access to the court system.

provides that a copy of any vexatious litigant order that is made must be served on all other relevant courts, so that other courts are aware of the order and can take appropriate action when receiving an application from the vexatious litigant.

provides that the Magistrates' and Children's Court must provide the Attorney-General with an annual report on the number of vexatious litigant orders made.  This is because this vexatious litigant power is usually only available to the Supreme Court and it is appropriate for the Attorney-General, as first law officer, to be advised of orders that limit access to the court system.

nodes.heading: PART 12—SERVICE OF DOCUMENTS
nodes.text: PART 12—SERVICE OF DOCUMENTS

outlines who must be provided with a copy of a family violence intervention order that is made, varied, extended or revoked by the court.  This is to ensure that all relevant persons and organisations are aware of the existence and terms of the order.

sets out how to serve documents that are required to be served on a person under this Bill.  However, clause 202(3) provides that the court may order substituted service or another form of service where it is not reasonably practicable to serve a document personally.  A family violence safety notice must be personally served.
sets out the documentation required to prove that service has occurred.  A certificate of service must be sworn or affirmed but if served by police or a court registrar may be certified.
provides that a certificate of service will be admissible as evidence and in the absence of evidence to the contrary will be proof of the matters stated in it.
states that if it has not been possible to serve a document a certificate of inability to serve must be filed with the court.

provides that if a person has the obligation under the Bill to serve or give a document, then the person may serve or give the document by causing it to be served or given by another person. For example, if a registrar of a court has an obligation to serve applications or orders made under the Bill, service is usually and lawfully carried out by police officers.
outlines the requirements for a police officer or court registrar when completing a certificate of service.

outlines when information may be obtained from certain public organisations for the purpose of service.  These provisions are to increase the likelihood of being able to locate a respondent for service.  This is particularly important for the service of family violence intervention orders, as an order may not be enforceable until it has been served.
states that this clause applies if a police officer is applying for information from an organisation to locate a respondent in order to serve a document under this Bill.
provides that the organisation must provide the information if it has it.

limits the scope of the information to be provided and the purpose it may be used for.  This is to ensure that the information is used only for the purpose of service and the respondent's privacy is protected to the greatest extent possible, while at the same time allowing service to occur.

nodes.heading: PART 13—MISCELLANEOUS Division 1—Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
nodes.text: PART 13—MISCELLANEOUS Division 1—Jurisdiction of Supreme Court

states that it is the intention of clauses 118 and 120 to alter or vary section 85 of the Constitution Act 1975.
Division 2—Rule-making power

provides a power for the Chief Magistrate together with two or more Deputy Chief Magistrates to jointly make rules for or with respect to proceedings brought in the Magistrates' Court under this Bill.  This clause also restates the power to issue practice directions, statements or notes for the court under section 16A of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.
lists matters which the court may make rules about but this provision does not limit the broad power given to the Magistrates' Court to make rules in clause 209(1).

provides that the President of the Children's Court together with two or more magistrates may jointly make rules for proceedings in that court in relation to applications under this Bill.  This clause also restates the power to issue practice directions, statements or notes for the court under section 592 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

enables such rules to be adopted or applied based on those made for the Magistrates' Court under clause 209. Clauses 210(4) and (5) enable the President of the Children's Court to issue practice directions, statements and notes to the Court under section 592 of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.
Division 3—Regulations
outlines the regulation-making power under the Bill.
sets out some matters that the regulations may prescribe but this list does not limit in any way the power to make regulations set out in clause 211(1).

nodes.heading: PART 14—REPEAL, TRANSITIONAL AND VALIDATION PROVISIONS Division 1—Repeal of Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987
nodes.text: PART 14—REPEAL, TRANSITIONAL AND VALIDATION PROVISIONS Division 1—Repeal of Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987

provides for the repeal of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987.
Division 2—Transitional and validation provisions

provides definitions for the transitional provisions.  Reference to the repealed Act means the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and reference to the new Act is the Bill.
The definitions of both interim orders and intervention orders refer to orders which protect a person from a family member and not orders made or varied under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 on grounds referred to in section 21A(5) of the Crimes Act 1958 which relate to stalking behaviour.
Commencement day for the purposes of Part 14 is defined to mean the day clause 213 commences operation.
provides that on and from commencement day, a reference in an Act or document to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 is taken, if the context permits, as a reference to the Bill.
provides transitional provisions for intervention orders relating to family violence under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987.
provides that on and after the commencement day, a final order relating to family violence made under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 is taken to be a final order under the Bill.
provides that on and after commencement day, an intervention order relating to family violence made under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 can be varied, revoked or extended under the Bill.
provides that on and after commencement day, an interim order relating to family violence made under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 is taken to be an interim order under the Bill.
provides that on and after commencement day, a counselling order under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 is taken to be a counselling order made under the Bill.

provides that if, immediately before the commencement day, an application was made for an intervention order on the grounds set out in section 4 or 4A of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987, but the proceedings had not yet started, then on and from the commencement day the application can be dealt with under the Bill.  Any special police immunities provided for in section 7A(2) of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and relied on by police  in those proceedings continue to apply to those proceedings.

provides if, immediately before the commencement day, proceedings for an application or an offence under section 22 of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 had commenced in a court but not concluded, the proceedings may continue as though the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 was still in force.

provides that if, immediately before commencement day, an interim order had been made on an application for an intervention order in respect of family violence, but the application had not been finally determined, the proceedings for the final determination may proceed as though the application and interim order were made under the Bill.

applies if after the commencement day a person applies for an intervention order against another person, but before the commencement day they would not have been considered family members under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987. The clause provides that the court may have regard to family violence committed before the commencement day when deciding whether to make the order.

provides that if an aggrieved family member under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 aided, abetted, counselled or procured the commission of a breach of an intervention order under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987, then whether or not the aggrieved family member had been charged under section 52 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 with an offence, clause 125 of the Bill applies to the aggrieved family member and they cannot be charged or if charged, the charges must be withdrawn.

provides that if an interstate protection order or New Zealand protection order has been registered in Victoria before the commencement, on and from that day, it is taken to be a final order under the Bill.

validates the registration of interstate orders under section 18AA of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987.  The effect of this clause is that all orders registered under section 18AA before the commencement of this clause are taken to be interstate summary protection orders within the definition in that Act, and to that extent, are validly registered under section 18AA.

nodes.heading: PART 15—REPEAL OF COUNSELLING ORDER PROVISIONS Division 1—Amendment of Family Violence Protection Act 2008
nodes.text: PART 15—REPEAL OF COUNSELLING ORDER PROVISIONS Division 1—Amendment of Family Violence Protection Act 2008

Clauses 225 to 232 have the effect of repealing Part 5 (Counselling Orders) and those provisions in the Bill and the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 which relate to the power of the courts to make counselling orders when final intervention orders are made in the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court.  Court ordered behaviour change counselling for those who have committed family violence is a trial program being conducted at Ballarat and Heidelberg Magistrates' Court.  At the conclusion of the trial on 30 June 2009, the relevant provisions of the Bill and Magistrates' Court Act 1989 will be repealed.  Depending on the evaluation of the trial, amendments may be required at a later date to the Bill to provide ongoing court powers to order behaviour change counselling.  Clause 231 is a transitional provision that ensures that even when the counselling provisions are repealed they continue to apply to any counselling orders made under the Bill before the repeal.
Division 2—Consequential amendment of Magistrates' Court Act 1989
repeals section 4I(1)(a)(ii) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 to remove references to counselling orders.

nodes.heading: PART 16—CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENTS Division 1—Amendment to the Bail Act 1977
nodes.text: PART 16—CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENTS Division 1—Amendment to the Bail Act 1977

makes a minor amendment to the Bail Act 1977 to refer to the Bill, and offences under it.
Division 2—Amendments to the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005

makes a minor amendment to the definition of child in the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 in order to include in the definition, in the case of a proceeding under the Bill, a person who is under the age of 18 when the application is made in the relevant proceedings.  This fills in a gap identified in the current definition.

amends the definition of proper venue in the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 to refer to proceedings under the Bill and inserts a definition of proper venue in relation to proceedings brought under the Bill.
makes a minor amendment to section 515(2) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, substituting reference to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 for a reference to the Bill.

makes a minor amendment to section 520C(3)(b) of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, substituting reference to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 for a reference to the Bill.
Division 3—Amendments to the Corrections Act 1986

substitutes paragraph (d)(ii) of the definition of victim in section 30A(1) of the Corrections Act 1986 to include a protected person under a final order under the Bill for which the prisoner or offender is the respondent.
makes a minor amendment to section 30C(3)(a) of the Corrections Act 1986 to reflect the change in terminology from "domestic violence" to "family violence".
amends section 60A of the Corrections Act 1986 to provide that certain persons are not eligible for home detention. Thus, persons who have been found guilty of—
a contravention of a final family violence intervention order under the Bill; or
a breach of an intervention order under the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987; or
an order of a corresponding nature made in another State or a Territory—
cannot have a home detention order made in respect of them.

substitutes section 60E(1)(l) of the Corrections Act 1986 to provide that a home detention assessment report must set out an assessment of the likelihood that a prisoner will commit an offence in respect of which a family violence intervention order could be made under the Bill.
Division 4—Amendments to the Crimes Act 1958

amends section 21A of the Crimes Act 1958 by inserting a new section 21A(5A).  It provides that, for the purposes of section 21A(5) of the Crimes Act 1958, the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 continues to apply, in the form it was in immediately prior to its repeal, as if it had not been repealed.  Any reference to a family violence intervention order in the Bill includes a reference to an intervention order made under section 21A(5) of the Crimes Act 1958.  Further, a reference in an Act to a contravention of a family violence intervention order under clause 123 of the Bill includes a reference to a breach of an intervention order referred to in section 21A(5).
Division 5—Amendments to the Evidence Act 1958

amends section 37C(2) of the Evidence Act 1958.  This section empowers a court to make alternative arrangements for the giving of evidence by a witness in particular proceedings. The amendments provide that a court may make such alternative arrangements where the proceeding relates, in whole or in part, to a charge for an offence where the conduct which constitutes the offence consists of family violence within the meaning of the Bill.

substitutes section 37CA(1) of the Evidence Act 1958 to provide that the section applies not only to proceedings for sexual offences, but also for offences where the conduct constituting the offence consists of family violence within the meaning of the Bill.
The clause also makes minor amendments to sections 37CA(5)(a) and 37CA(10) of the Evidence Act 1958 to make clear that information and warnings to the jury must only be given if there is a jury.
Division 6—Amendments to the Firearms Act 1996

substitutes paragraph (c)(i) of the definition of prohibited person in section 3(1) of the Firearms Act 1996 in order to remove reference to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and replace this reference with reference to the Bill.
makes minor amendments to references to subsections in section 49 of the Firearms Act 1996.

makes minor amendments section 53(4)(a) of the Firearms Act 1996.  These amendments are required in order to insert references to the Bill.  The clause also makes minor changes to the time periods specified in the section, consistent with recent amendments to the Firearms Act 1996.

substitutes section 189(1) of the Firearms Act 1996.  The clause enables a person who deemed to be a prohibited person, due to the fact that they are subject to an intervention order under the Bill, to apply to a court for a declaration that they are deemed—
not to be a prohibited person by virtue of this fact; or
is so deemed for limited purposes only.

However, such a person must not apply for a declaration if the intervention order revoked any licence, permit or other authority to possess, carry or use firearms.
The clause also inserts section 189(4) into the Firearms Act 1996.  This clause provides that an application under section 189(1) may not be made until any appeal under the Bill has been determined.

inserts a new section 211 into the Firearms Act 1996.  This new section is a transitional provision which deals with the relationship between the Bill, the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and the Firearms Act 1996. Division 7—Amendment to the Health Records Act 2001

makes minor amendments to the definition of law enforcement function in section 3(1) of the Health Records Act 2001 to substitute a reference to the Bill.
Division 8—Amendments to the Magistrates' Court Act 1989
makes minor amendments to the definitions section of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.

amends the definition of family violence contained in section 3(1) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 to make it the same as the definition contained in the Bill.
The clause also substitutes the definition of party in order to replace references to the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with references to the Bill.
of the Bill also amends the definition of proper venue to give greater flexibility and accessibility to the courts.

makes minor amendments to section 4F(1)(b)(ii) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, which relates to the Koori Court Division of the Magistrates' Court.  These amendments are required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.

makes minor amendments to section 4I(1)(a) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, which relates to the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court.  These amendments are required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.
Clauses 253(3) and (4) of the Bill make minor amendments to section 4L of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, which relates to the Family Violence Court Division of the Magistrates' Court. These amendments are required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.  In particular, the amendments are required in order to reflect the change in terminology from "intervention order or interim intervention order" to "family violence intervention order".

Clause 254(1) of the Bill makes minor amendments to section 4O(2)(b) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, which relates to the Neighbourhood Justice Division of the Magistrates' Court. These amendments are required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.
Likewise, clause 254(2) of the Bill makes minor amendments to section 4O(3)(e) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, which relates to the Neighbourhood Justice Division of the Magistrates' Court.  These amendments are required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.

makes a minor amendment to section 1A(4)(f) of Schedule 2 to the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.  This amendment is required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.
Division 9—Amendment to the Police Regulation Act 1958

makes a minor amendment to item 3.3 of the First Schedule to the Police Regulation Act 1958.  This amendment is required in order to reflect the replacement of the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 with the Bill.
Division 10—Amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act 1997
amends section 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to insert the definitions of exclusion condition, family violence intervention order and family violence safety notice into that Act.
amends section 70(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 so that it refers to both sections 70A (see clause 303) and 71 of that Act.

inserts new section 70A into the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.  New section 70A is designed to allow a person who is protected by an exclusion condition of a family violence intervention order or a family violence safety notice to change the locks of their residential premises without being obliged to give a copy of the key to the excluded party, even if that person is a party to the tenancy agreement.
The protected party will still be obliged to give a copy of the new key to any other parties to the tenancy agreement, including the landlord or the landlord's agent. The protected party must also give a certified extract of the family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order or a full copy of the notice or order to the landlord or the landlord's agent.  The landlord or landlord's agent must not give a copy of the key to the excluded party for the duration of the exclusion condition.
The purpose of giving a copy or certified extract of the family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order to the landlord or the landlord's agent is to ensure that the landlord or landlord's agent knows that there is a legal basis for refusing to give a copy of a key to the excluded party for the duration of the exclusion condition.  It effectively puts the landlord or landlord's agent "on notice" of their obligations.
A family violence intervention order or family violence safety notice is a very sensitive document that contains personal information.  For this reason, new section 70A(7) provides that the landlord may only disclose or give a copy of family violence intervention order or family violence safety notice (or a certified extract of the order or notice) obtained under this section to the landlord's agent.  The same obligation is imposed on the landlord's agent vis-à-vis the landlord.  In each case the documents can be disclosed or given to a relevant legal representative or any other person who is prescribed.

amends section 86 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to provide a new circumstance in which a landlord or landlord's agent may inspect a residential premises.  This amendment will allow a landlord or landlord's agent to inspect a residential premises where an application has been made to terminate an existing tenancy agreement and create a new tenancy agreement because a party to the tenancy agreement has been excluded from the premises under an exclusion condition in a final family violence intervention order (see new section 233A).
The purpose of this new inspection power is to allow any issues of damage to the property to be resolved if the Tribunal elects to terminate an existing tenancy agreement, and create a new, tenancy agreement under new section 233B.  This will mean that liability for damage to the property that occurred under the original tenancy agreement will be attributed to the parties to that original tenancy agreement.  Parties to the new lease will not assume liability for that damage under the new tenancy agreement.  This provision does not allow an assessment for compensation for early termination of the tenancy agreement. The excluded party will not be able to attend the inspection because of the exclusion condition.  However, new subsection 86(4) allows the excluded party to have a representative present at the inspection.  This is to protect the interests of the excluded party in the event of any dispute regarding damage to the residential premises.  For example, it would allow the excluded party's representative to take photographs of alleged damage to the residential premises in case the excluded party wished to contest the extent of damage to the residential premises. It would not allow the excluded party's representative to take photographs, for example, of personal items present in the residential premises that were unrelated to questions of damage to the residential premises.

amends section 88 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to provide that if an inspection of a residential premises is made under new subsection 86(4), the notice of inspection provided to the protected party (and other tenants at the premises) must include the name of the protected person's representative (if any) in addition to the usual details of how the inspection will take place.

inserts new sections 233A, 233B, 233C and 233D into the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.
Section 233A allows a person who is protected by an exclusion condition in a final order to apply to have an existing tenancy agreement terminated and a new tenancy agreement created where the excluded tenant is a party to the original tenancy agreement and the protected person is also a party to the that agreement or has been living in the rented premises as their principal place of residence.  Final order has the same meaning as in section 11 of the Bill.
The purpose of this is to provide a mechanism to align the tenancy agreement with the practical and legal reality of who may live in the property if one of the tenants is excluded from a residential property under the conditions of a final order.
The parties to the application are any parties to the existing lease, including the protected person, the excluded tenant, the landlord or landlord's agent and any co-tenants (in respect of the termination of the existing tenancy agreement) and the protected person, any other persons who are applying to live in the property and the landlord or the landlord's agent (in respect of the creation of the new tenancy agreement). The protected person may apply to live with one or more persons under the new tenancy agreement.  For example, a protected person may wish to assume a new tenancy agreement jointly with their sister or friend, to help with the rent.
New section 233B provides that the Tribunal may terminate the existing tenancy agreement and create a new agreement if it is satisfied of certain things.  The Tribunal must be satisfied that—
the proposed new tenants could reasonably be expected to comply with the tenancy agreement—this is designed to prevent unviable tenancies from being created;

the protected person or their dependent children would be likely to suffer severe hardship if they were required to leave the premises—for example, the Tribunal may consider the trauma that may result from a victim of family violence being required to leave their social support network; children being required to leave their school or the difficulty that the protected person may have in finding new rental accommodation;
the hardship suffered by the protected person would be greater than any hardship that the landlord may suffer;
it is reasonable to do so given the length of the exclusion condition and the length of the lease;

it is reasonable to do so given the interests of co-tenants (other than the excluded party)—for example, if a co-tenant were disadvantaged by the application to end the tenancy agreement, this is a relevant consideration for the Tribunal.  In particular, the Tribunal will consider whether the co-tenants support the application to terminate the tenancy agreement and create a new one.

If the Tribunal elects to make a new tenancy agreement, it must be subject to the same rent and frequency of rent payments as the original agreement.  The termination date for the agreement should not be later than that which applied under the original agreement.  That is, if the original agreement was for a fixed term of one year and had three months yet to run, the new agreement must be for no longer than three months.  Otherwise, the new tenancy agreement must be on the same terms and conditions as the original agreement, subject to any changes that the Tribunal determines. New section 233B(3) provides that if the Tribunal makes an order under new section 233B(1), the existing tenancy agreement expires on the signing of the new one.
New section 233C allows the Tribunal to determine the liabilities of the excluded tenant, protected person and any other tenant under the existing tenancy agreement.
