To do so, the Tribunal may adjourn the hearing to allow an inspection of the rented premises under the new section 86(1)(g) (see clause 260(2)).
New section 233D is designed to minimise, to the greatest extent possible, the trauma that a protected person may face by being personally cross-examined by the respondent to the final order whilst preserving natural justice.
The Victorian Civil and Administration Tribunal (VCAT) has an inherent power to determine how proceedings are conducted under the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998.  However, section 233D specifically provides that an excluded tenant must not personally cross-examine a protected person unless the Tribunal grants leave to do so.  This clause does not restrict a person acting on behalf of the excluded tenant, from cross-examining the protected person.
If the excluded tenant is permitted to personally cross-examine the protected person, they can only do so if their cross-examination is directly relevant to the matter at hand. They cannot use the cross-examination to re-open questions about the nature of the family violence that the protected person experienced or any other irrelevant matter.

amends section 234 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to clarify that the making of a family violence intervention order (interim or final) that contains an exclusion condition may result in severe hardship for a tenant under a fixed term tenancy agreement.
This severe hardship may arise if the tenant is excluded from the residential premises and is nevertheless required to pay rent under the tenancy agreement (for example, if the excluded tenant cannot afford to pay rent on the premises from which they are excluded and a new premises and so is at risk of homelessness). Severe hardship may also arise if a protected person is a tenant but wishes to break the tenancy agreement so that the excluded tenant no longer knows where they live to protect their safety or the safety of their children.

amends section 506 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 to provide for the means by which documents may be served on an excluded tenant under that Act.  These provisions are designed to make allowance for the fact that a person may be excluded from their last known address and may not have a fixed address. For example, a person may provide an address to the Court under clause 85 of the Bill that may be an email address.
Division 11—Amendments to the Sentencing Act 1991

amends section 18ZV of the Sentencing Act 1991 to provide that certain persons are not eligible for home detention. Thus, persons who have been found guilty of a contravention of a family violence intervention order or family violence safety notice under the Bill or an order of a corresponding nature made in another State or a Territory cannot have a home detention order made in respect of them.

substitutes section 99G(1)(l) of the Sentencing Act 1991 to provide that a home detention assessment report must set out an assessment of the likelihood that a prisoner will commit an offence in respect of which a family violence intervention order could be made under the Bill.

Division 13—Amendments to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998

inserts a new section 62A into the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998.  This new section will enable a protected person or respondent to a family violence intervention order to be accompanied by a support person at a hearing of a proceeding under the Bill.  The purpose of the support person is to provide support to the protected person or respondent.  The clause also sets out the types of people who may act as support persons.

inserts new clauses 73A and 73B into Schedule 1 of the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998. Clause 73A prohibits a respondent from personally cross-examining a protected person (under the same family violence intervention order) unless the Tribunal gives the respondent leave to do so.  This is designed to protect the protected person from threatening or harassing behaviour by the respondent which may be achieved through aggressive cross examination on irrelevant issues.
Clause 73B of Schedule 1 enables the Tribunal to direct the making of any of a number of enumerated alternative arrangements for the purpose of a witness giving evidence in a proceeding.  The Tribunal may vary or revoke a direction under this clause at any time, on its own initiative or on the application of a party to the proceeding (see clause 73B(6)).
Clause 73B(5) of the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998 provides that any place outside the hearing room where a witness may give evidence is taken to be part of the hearing room while the witness is there for the purposes of giving evidence.  Clause 73B(7) defines hearing room as the room in which the hearing for the proceedings is being conducted.
Clause 73B(2) of the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998 provides that, in the case of adult witnesses, the Tribunal may make such a direction on its own initiative or on the application of a party to the proceeding.
Clause 73B(3) of the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998 provides that the Tribunal must make such a direction if a witness is under 18 years of age unless the Tribunal does not consider it appropriate, taking into account—
the wishes of the witness; and
the age and maturity of the witness; and
any other matters the Tribunal considers relevant.

Clause 73B(4) of the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 1998 enables the Tribunal to hear applications or ascertain the matters in clause 73B(3) in camera.  Persons who are not parties to the proceeding (or their representatives) may not be present during these times, unless the Tribunal directs otherwise.
Division 14—Amendment to the Working with Children Act 2005

makes a minor amendment to the Working with Children Act 2005.  This amendment is required in order to reflect the fact that the relevant definition of domestic partner is now located in the Relationships Act 2008, not the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987.
Division 15—Repeal of the Magistrates' Court (Family Violence) Act 2004

provides for the repeal of the Magistrates' Court (Family Violence) Act 2004, which amended the Crimes (Family Violence) Act 1987 and provided for the repeal of the counselling order provisions in that Act.  These repeal provisions are re-enacted in Part 15 of this Bill, and the rest of the 2004 Act has commenced.  The 2004 Act is therefore spent and can be safely repealed.
